div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

The statement which has appeared in several of the MY DEAR NELLIE, London papers lately, to the effect that Her Majesty in- tends visiting Ireland next year. is incorrect, but the At this time of the year party smocks and frocks Prinee and Princess of Wales, or the Duke and Duchess are naturally of first importance, and for little of York will, it is announced, spend some weeks in the girls of from five to ten years no style of dress ix Emerald Isle, during the summer of 1897. Their Royal more artistic and becoming than the time,honoured Highnesses are to be the guests of Lord and Lady Cada- smock, falling straight from the yoke, which may gan at Dublin, and they will pay a series of country- be either smocked or plain as fancy dictates. A house visits in the northein, southern and western coon- pretty smock suitable for a child of from four to ties. The Queen has paid three visits to Ireland, one in eight years, may be made in soft silk or of fine 1849, another in 1853, and the last in 1861, just a few nun's veiling or cashmere; in cream, pale blue, or months before the death of the Prince Consort. There pink, and trimmed with white, blonde, or Brussels was one other visit of an English Sovereign to Ireland,in lace. Party smocks, whether of milk or cashmere, the present century, that of George W. in 1821. should not be lined, merely turned up with a deep The removal of the Court from Windsor to Osborne, necessitates, owing to the sea passage an enormous hem at the bottom. They are worn over cambric : or nainsook petticoats, trimmed with frills of amount of trouble hich ot ualls pp ted by Her Majesty's houLhwold, eslspenci ‘4B if theaw. e_ ar te hme ar Valenciennes ace. favourable. And the same trouble continues during the' :se whole stay of the Queen in the Isle ef Wight, for despite the fact thee one of the Royal yachts is always under steam at Trinity Pier, East Cowes, ready to start when the Osborne telephone commands, even so narrow a strip of water as the Spithead Solent Channel, makes a wonderful difference in the communication with Wind- sor, which is practically the Royal headquarters. Although we are most of us aware of Her Majesty's disliketo the odour of the " fragrant weed," the fact that the majority of the crowned female heads of Europe are notorious for their davotion to tobacco, is not so generally known. The Dowager Empress of Russia, un- like the young Czarina, who shares the Queen's ideas on the subject, is a great smoker, the Empress of Austria consumes between forty and fiftv cigarettes every day, while the Queen of Roumania, the Queen of Italy, the Queen Regent of Spain, and the Queen of Portugal, are all practised smokers. Although Bagshot House, near Aldershot) whero the Duke and Duchess of Connaught have both been lying ill, ought, if the condition of the soil be taken into con- sideration, to be situated in a singularly favourable locality, the climate varying between extreme heat in summer and great cold in winter, the fact remains that it has never agreed with the Duchess, and on her re- covery Her Royal Highness will once more visit the Riviera, possibly accompanied by the Duke. For many years the mansion was lent by the Queen to her favourite physician, Sir James Clarke, but he always took good care tolgo away to Bournemouth or the South of France,in the winter and early spring. Not many of us realise, while the busy postmen are scampering from door to door leaving at almost every one whole showers of dainty Christmas cards that al- ready the designs of cards destined for Christmas 1897 are in preparation. All the designs must be ready by May, then they pass into the hands of the makers, and by October the cards must be ready for the shops. And speaking of that useful and always (or nearly always) welcome individual the postman, reminds me f a delicious example of the frequent idiocy of Post Office red tape. A rural specimen in the West of England happened just lately to become possessed of a pony,and net unnaturally came to the conclusion that he might just as well uldise the animal for the purpose of going his rounds. The pony cost nobody but its owner one penny piece, and the delivery of the letters was acele- rated, but red tape, in the shape of the postmistress stepped in and dismounted the man. "He was only a walking postman,and had no business to ride," the lady remarked. It would be interesting to know what would have become of the unfortunate man if he had ventured to run, or ride a bicycle! A house to house delivery of letters has recently been inaugirated in Johannesburg, but from a Transvaal paper just to hand it could scarcely be termed a suc- cess. It seems it is impossible to rat-tat-tat after the usual approved faahion, because knockers are!unknown in those parts, and as many of the houses are not num- bered and the residents themselves have no idea at whet number they reside, it is calculated that each early morning delivery will be completed about mid- night, until a few fresh arrangements are made. More- over, it appears that in a large number of cases, the postmen have been treated under a mistaken idea of their mission, to the warm welcome usually accorded to the process-server. Although led has been the favourite colour this win- ter among all upeto-date women, Royalty so far, has shewn no preference for it, but then Roy alty seldom goes. with the multitude, in fashion. The Princess of Wales has been wearing petunia very much of late, and there is little doubt that few women can don this particular colour as successfully as Her Royal Highnesa, Hitherto petunia has been manufactured only in the most ex- pensive cloths, but it is now obtain Able in ordinary double width serge. , The verylprettiest ball gowns I have espied lately for young girls wear, are built of tulle, scattered over with tiny flowers to match, can be had all ready to slip over the low bodice and needless to say they are in consider- able request now there are fie many festivities in pros- pect. It appears likely that in a few years time there will hardly be any but artificial fur procurable, as in many parts of the world and particularly in North America, it is well-known the fur-bearing animals are only found in greatly diminished numbers, and in like manner the fur-bearing seal is fast disappearing from the seas. There is row, it is said, scarcely a seal to be found along the Western Coast of the North American Continent where formerly it used to resort in great numbers, for thou- sands of miles round the coast. For years past there has been a considerable falling off in the number of seals slaughtered each season, but it is stated the ships em- ployed can now only pay their expenses by greatly putting up their prices. Many, however, would wel- come the total abandonment of the trade, as there is no doubt whatever, that it involves great cruelty to one of the most harmless of animals. It may interest some of my readers to know that the use of the mistletoe at Christmas in the embellishment oi our houses, finds its origin in some aneient beliefs held ty the ancient Germans and Britains. according to art old tradition the cross used at the Crucifixion was con- structed from a mistletoe tree which then flourished in the forest, but after that, it only existed in the parisi- tical form in which we know it now. It was also credited by the ancient Britains with the power of heal- ing various diseases, and there is still a custom in North- ern Europe of wearing rings and armulets, constructed of the wood as a charm against sickness. By far the largest quantity of mistletoe is imported from Brittany and Normandy, and during the past week or two, hun- dreds of huge crates filled with white-berried branches have been eonveyed from St. Maio to Southampton. The trade grows larger every year, and long before our sup- plies are needed, baskets are being despatched to Aus- tralia, and other colonies. • CHRISTMAS PUDDING SANDWICHES are delicious. Take some cold plum pudding and cut it into wafer-like slices, and place them between thin slices of brown or malt bread, well buttered. These who like very sweet sand- wiches should natter a little castor sugar over the pud ding before making the sandwiches.
"WOMEN'S CHAT!'

A warm and suitable jacket for a young lady of about 15 or 16 can be made of blue cloth, double- breasted, hemmed with black astrachan, and fitted for winter wear, is of thoroughly warm thick cloth, and the hat to match this might be of fine white felt with s border of rough felt trimmed with waving white plumes and a black osprey tied with black satin ribbons. -Even those girls who have so fatal a knack of unbecoming a hat, would look well under the influence of this. A handsome mantle for a matron has a straight front and fitting dolman back of black lisreine plush, and the cape-like or " bell " sleeves of matelassd with petunia silk design. A box-pleat of the matelasse goes down the front, and the mantle is trimmed with black thibet fleece. The materials required are one and a-half yards each of double width lisreine and matelasse, five yards of satin or four of polonvise for lining, five yards of three or four inch thibet, and half a yard of wider (for the collar).

A neat and ladylike costume is made of fancy blue material, trimmed on the epaulettes and cuffs with narrow rouleaux of black satin; a wide black satin belt goes round the waist, and is fastened with jet buckles, and black satin points,, veiled with creamy lace, go over the shoulders. With this is worn a very stylish toque, with a fashionable high gown. Walking gowns of cloth made with a coat and skirt to match are the latest fashions in Paris. One novel example is in blue cloth with a loose sacque coat, cut short and rounded under the arms somewhat in the style of a bolero, giving it the appearance of stole ends back and front. Two square tabs are cut on at each shoulder to fall over the sleeves, and the fronts are lined with chinchilla, which gives the effect of revers when the coat is open. • All the edges are handsomely braided with black, and the skirt of the gown is cut in scallops on the bottom to show a plaiting of red silk, and each one is braided.
" MADGE."

There are some lovely felt hats to be got now. and these, trimmed with narrow rows of black ribbon velvet, fastened with tiny paste buckles, look most becoming. On the right side are some beautiful white ostrich tips, with white ospreys mixed in, and clusters of pink and white roses. The brim is turned up slightly on the left side, with some more white and pink roses.

Empire belts and belts of all sorts are the most conspicuous detail of dress this season, with the exception, of course, of the little bolero, and aiey are made of satin and velvet and embroidered with beads, covered with an applique of a contrasting colour or draped plain as you wish. Some have a narrow double box plaited frill in the upper edges, and others have a deep fringe at the bottom, but the most becoming belt is shaped wide under the arms and tapers down at the back and front. Leather belts are alt very narrow, and the very latest novelty is bright scarlet. Hero c are a few facts about sleeves which are now worn very long, and which is quite a discom- fort to many, but is becoming to those whose hands are not their strong point. The tendency of the new sleeves is to diTlay the contour of the arm from the wrist to the shoulder. That the sleeve will be the coat sleeve of the future is hardly to be doubted. Fashion is "letting us down" gently by a little trimming at the top now, but soon this will all be gone. Spring will show. . A pretty fashion for the bottom of a sleeve is to have it slashed or 'Vandyke' points with a ruffle of lace or accordeon-pleated chin') under it. The ; puffs at the top of the sleeves are not now stif- felled. The more individual the style, and the ; more befurbelowecl the sleeve, the more chic is the costume considered.
Your loving JENNIM.

div.head: WHY THE PHYSICIAN IS WELL.
div.p: WHY THE PHYSICIAN IS WELL.

Did you ever consider why it is that physicians so seldom suffer with the many ailments of other persons? At first thought you might think it is because physicians have many kinds of drugs at hand, and can take them as often as they like. Yet this thought shoots wide of the mark, because it there is one thing the physician does not do, it is to keep dosing himself with drugs. When be is really ill be goes to bed, and sends for a drictor in whom he has confidence, just as any other sane person ought to do. The physician of ti-day has greater faith in Nature han the physician of last century. He prescribes drugs when necessary, but the whole enlightened medical pro- fession of our time emphasises the importance of good care and the right kind of nourishment. Careful living and nourishment are the key to the good health you expect, and usually and, in the physician's own family. Our correspondence shows us that many physicians throughout this vast empire use Scott's Emulsion in their families. What better endorsement of a prepara- tion could there be than. this? The physician knpws that Scott's Emulsion is the easiest, best, most palatable, and most reliable form of cod-liver oil, combined with the hypophosphites of lime and soda. He knows that the oil in Scott's Emulsion is of the highest grade that Norway produces, and is free from decomposition, and consequent rancidity. He understands what it means to health to have the nourishing properties of this remedy. Scott's Emulsion is not a secret Preparation. The label on every genuine bottle tells what it contnins. For comsumptives, aeremics, weak children, nd all those whose pale cheeks and thinness shoe!. a want of vitality and strength, Scott's Emulsion I. of especial ad- vantage ; and it is also an admirable. remedy for coughs, colds, bronchitis, and local inflammation of throat and lunge. A nurse, in writing of net experience in the case

of a weak baby, says : " My little grandd^.aghter, Alice Maud, has derived great benefit from the use of Scott's Emulsion. At the age of four months she was dreadfully weak and emaciate. I was almost at a loss to know what to do, when to August last a friend of mire recommended S:,ott's Emulsion, and after trying two hal f-crown bottles the result was simply marvellous. I still continued it for nearly six months, and she is now perfectly healthy and strong, which you may judge by the, photo I send. ' Being a nurse, I strongly recommend Scott's Emulsion wherever I see any need of it, and there are many cases I coUld tell you of that have derived great benefit fr)in its use. I remain inrs,yours gratefully, (,ignet") JESSIE GEORGE, 26, Cabholm Terrace, Chbhoun 1-lactl, South- town, May 4th 1896.

By the Author of " The' Double Life,' " Ths Bailiff's Scheme,' Ste., &o.

CHAPTER %XXVI. UNSEALING THE GRAVE. Sir Graham Gallagher was seated by one of the long French windows overlooking the mere. He arose at Lord Champney's entrance, and came for- ward with outstretched hands, his patriarchal face beaming. - The baron welcomed him cordially. "It seems an age since 1 saw you last, my dear Sir Graham !" he exclaimed, his dark face lighting with a friendly glow. "It is an age," declared the court physician. "We have not met since hady Champney's memor- able illness seventeen years ago. And since then you have served our country at a foreign court and have changed from the impetuous boy—you were little more then, if you were married—into a grave, dignified and stately man." Lord Charnpney uttered a sigh. "And you, he responded, letting fall the phy- sician's hand, and motioning him to return to his seat—" you have changed also. You have added a title to your name, ;led are known as one of the first in your profession. Yet life may have dealt as hardly with you, after all, as with me. This brilliant success in material things may cover an uneasy, or a broken heart. Y-eu have an anxious, troubled, preoccupied look—" "It is not for myself," interposed Sir Graham, who was meditating upon the best plan of breaking to his host the news he had brought. "Life has been bountiful tome. My home is pleasant, my wife affectionate and sympathizing, my children all well settled in life. lam contented—happy." Lord Champney looked at his guest wistfully.. "You have drawn prizes in the great lotterS, of life," he muttered. "And I-1 have drawn blanks !" The stately old court physician, leaning his chin on the top of his staff, looked at his host wonder- ingly. "Blanks I" he repeated, glancing around the elegant apartment. "Blanks—with such a home! with such a name I With the fairest, queenliest. wife in the land t" There was something in the old doctor's manner that touched the spring of Lord Champney's griefs —something so paternal, so kindly; that he was tempted to tell him all his miserable story. "You think I am to be envied, Sir Graham," he said, bitterly; "but I am the most unhappy. man In the kingdom. What comfort does it afford me that I am called a successful minister, an accom- plished diplomat? My nature is more domestic than ambitious. I have had no home for seven- teen years. I have been restless, jealous, suspicious, unhappy, accursed." Sir Graham's face was full of concern and sym- pathy. "It is possible?" he asked. "I knew that you lived abroad, and that Lady Champney lived in seclusion on her estate of Saltair. But I never dreamed of this state of affairs between you. I supposed that you made frequent visits home, and that her ladyship's health did not permit a foreign residence. I thought that, your ambition was paramount. What could have brought about such a terrible estrangemeast, my dear baron?" And the kindly old physician drew his chair closer to that of his moody, miserable host. "There is not in all England a purer and more discreet lady than your wife. It cannot be that you have ceased to love each other ?" "Yes—no," answered Lord Chempney, stem- meringly. "Pardon me, Sir Graham, but even to you I cannot talk over this matter. It is enough to say that I Jove my wife a thousandfold better than in the old days when you knew us. But at heart we are dead to each other. It is as Lady Chatnpney said to me on my arrival at Saltair— there is a grave between us. "A grave?" "Yes, the grave of our little child. She buried- her love for me with that little creature. And, to show you how completely I am dead to her, she said to me that when I could restore to her the child that had never nestled in her bosom, then she would be to me all that she had been—all that I desired." Sir Graham's eyes widened. A sudden glow burned on his wrinkled cheeks. A strange light beamed from his eyes. "Her ladyship said that r ' he asked, eagerly. "Yes—but can one bring back the dead? Can one clothe again in flesh the little mouldering bones? As easy as to kindle in her cold heart the old dead love! I cannot give her child' back to her here, but perhaps I may in the hereafter. She does not dream, Sir Graham, that I, too, have mourned for that little lost one. She forgets, in her mother anguisn, that the father, too, is bercft and sorrowful. In my lonely moments there often comes to me the vision of that little angel. She was more to me than my daughter. She was the link that bound me to my wife. And she died among stranger;, and her mother's eyes never saw her.' A sudden agitation seized the old court physi..

"God my soul I" he ejaculated, springing up and walking to and fro in great haste, and wip- ing his spectacles. "I never heard anything like this! And here are two healthy people fretting themselves to death for a trifle 1" "A trifle, Sir Graham?" demanded the baron, indignantly. "A mere trifle !" responded Sir Graham, ex- citedly. "I'll tell you what to do, my lord. Put yourself under my orders, and I'll engage to restore your domestic harmony. You must do as Lady Champney said—give her back her daughter." Lord Champney began to think that his guest had gone mad. "Does the grave give up its dead?' he asked. "Not as I know of—at least, not alive. But strange things sometimes happen, my lord. You've no idea of the astounding iniquities sometimes perpetrated. This world is a gigantic fraud—at least, the people in it are. Bless my soul! I've just got track of the strangest fraud I ever heard of. You 'd be astonished if I were to tell you of it —but that is what I am here for. Are you per. fectly calm, Baron ?" Lord Champney's private opinion in regard to the state of the old doctor's mind became still more unfavourable. He replied to Sir Graham's question in the affiimative, and in a soothing voice. Sir Graham continued his excited walk, his face Cushing to the hue of a peony, and his air that of one burdened with a great secret. "It 'a a queer story, as I believe I said," resumed the old court physician. "This is where it begins. Last night, about midnight, when my family had retired, 1 was sitting alone in my study consulting the authorities about a very interesting case I have on hand. In the midst of my work I heard a low moan, and a sound as of some one falling on the grass outside my window. Iran out —and what should I see but a young girl? I picked her up and took her into the house. As I bei.rd some one howling after her in my garden, and as the affair looked mysterious, I just dropped my curtain to shut out intruders and then to work to recover the young girl, who was in a dead faint." " Well ?'" said the baron, ws,ndering if the doctor's insanity were not, after all, the dotage of old-age. "What is all tl•,is to me, if I may be allowed to ask, Sir Grs!Am?" "Wait !"conimar,deii the exited doctor. "Have patience, my he a. As I was bending over this young girl bar torn sleeve fell back from her arm, and I sa.n on the right arm—mind you, the right arm, e:-.4.d ab,,ve the elbow—a peculiar mark. It was a small, oddly shaped cross, consisting only of two lines of bright scarlet crossing each other irregularly " The baron started. "Too mark was like that of my little dead Bar- bara ?" he exe'simed. "An odd coincidence." "Yea, I shoald think so. Bless my soul l—a very odd ceieeidence. Well. the girl came to, and she told me her whole pitiful story. She was as beautiful as an aogel, with a little restless head (nivel ed ali over with tiny clinging curls—just the colour of your bail as true as life V' ejaculated Sir Graham, pausing to contemplate his host, after an excited fashion. "She was as slender as a sylph, with a pure, child like face, and big, innocent, sweet eyes, and a piteous look. And, somehow, she reminded me of you. Your child, if she had lived, would have been the imago of that girl, my lord." " Indeed 1" said, the baron, cold!y, and not well pleased at the alhilin. " And who did this midnight wanderer—this romantic young lady— prove to be ?" "She said that the ohllTieate I had hesrli pur- suing her was her Mother. :!•!.hP aid that this mother had sold her in her intaney to a kind old Sussex squire, who had braugh. bi:r up as his daueter, given her every aceinci,,i..noilut, petted her and loved her—in short, at the: I);atsBe goes, made a lady. of her."
II3ER iB. •

"A poor- speculation on the part of the Sussex ; squire, observed Lord Champney, trying to hide a yawn. "This educating people above their station in life isn't so very commendable. It appears that events drove the girl back to tho protection of her own mother." "The squire died without a will, leaving the girl penniless. The squire's son, an avaricious young man about to marry, gave her a sum of money, and told her that she must go with her mother; and she went. The mother took her to London, where the father joined them. Imagine the position of this young girl. A lady by in- stinct and education, refined, delicate, and pure as the mountain snow, tied to these parents of hers—a sordid, avaricious, ignorant, drunken couple, who meant to .make her support them, honourably or dishonourably. as the case might be." Lord Champney shuddered. "Poor girl 1" he said. "You did right to come, to me, Sir Graham. Put my name down for any amount necessary—" The court physician put up his hand depreca- tingly. ' "Let me finish," he exclaimed. " This girl had two lovers down in Sussex; one of them a country squire; a young gentleman with a university edu- cation ; the other, a fine city gallant, who stopped at Horsham." "Why, that's where Felix—Felix Warner—you remember him, Sir Graham—has been stopping so long 1" "The -fine gallant visited her in London," con- tinued the doctor, his excitement beginning to abate, and to give place to an anxious restless-. ness, as he watched his unconscious host, "and finding that she was no longer an heiress, and that she had such relatives, he made her infamous proposals—" "The dastardly wretch The miserable cow- ard 1" cried Lord Champney, whose fine sense of honour and strict ideas of justice were aroused to a , violent pitch of indication against the base suitor. "Of course she dismissed the fellow ?" " Yes ; but these parents of hers favoured his in- famous suit, and the girl fled from them. They recaptured her and took her down to Chiswick, to a cottage in the rear of my gardens. Her per- secutor came there last night, and found her shut up in an upper room. He threatened her, and went down stairs. The girl then managed to escape by the window, and got over into my gar- den, with the whole infamous pack after her, and she fell fainting before my window, and I took

her in." "And she is at your house now?" "No. I went to call Lady Gallagher, and when I returned the girl was gone. I haven't seen her since!" Lord Champney smiled cynically. "Ahl" he said, significantly. And were your silver stands, and gold pens and other costly trifles gout: too?" "No, my lord. The girl had evidently been frightened away, or summoned by this young squire—her country lover—who had helped her to weave. She was no impostor—l'll stake my life on that." "Your faith in human nature is pleasant to wit- ness," said the baron, half smiling, half sighing. "You don't want help for her, since she has dis- appeared? Why, then, have you come to me with this story, my dear Sir Graham ?" The physician took a hurried turn or two around the room. "You canßot guess ?" he then asked "Not I. Unless," said Lord Champney, with a sudden start and an incredulous smile, "you mean that you would like me to find this girl, and, taking advantage of the odd coincidence of the birth-mark, present her to Lady Champney as our daughter, about the statement of whose death there was some strange mistake ?" Sir Graham stopped short. "That is just what I mean 1" he said. Lord Champney stared. "You are insane, then 1" he exclaimed, involun-

tarily. "Not at all ; " and Sir Graham smiled. "See how easily the thing could be done. The girl looks like you and your wife. She bears the same mark that your child bore. She is not the daughter of these people who claim her—" "Not their daughter 2" "No. I know she isn't. She knows it. The couple rented a small farm many years ago in Suirey. The woman had been lady's maid to a doctor's wife. The doctor out of pity and kindly interest, recommended her as nurse to a noble family, and the little noble heiress was sent to her and placed in their charge. The man soon after committed a forgery—" • At this point the baron sprang up, electrifled. "You mean that this young girl, then, is their nurse-child, and not their own offspring ?" " Yes—l maan that 1" "The names—the name of this couple 1" "John and Catherine Narr !" The barou looked at the physician in dumb amazement. Then, a little later, he broke the hush by a whin:if : "My God you mean that the girl is mine— feally mine—my own daughter 2" Sir Graham nodded gravely. Again the baron was speechless. He leaned against the mantel-piece, his face strangely white, his st.:.rn lips quivering. "Have I not broken the news gently enough?' asked the physician, with an anxious smile. My lord, there has been some gross fraud in this matter. The girl who was in my house last night, and who is claimed by the Narrs as their child, is really and truly the daughter you have so long mourned as dead I I will stake my life on the truth of this statement I" "it would be a bliss too great for belief 1" mur- mured the baron. "No such joy as this would be in store for me." "Bless n,v soul!" cried Sir Graham, impatiently. "You act Like a man in a trance, my lord. Rouse yourself.. There is no grave between you and your wife now. Lord Champney looked up, dazed and bewildered. He could not comprehend, even yet, his great cause for joy. "I must go and tell Barbara," he said, taking a step towards the door. "Not so," said the physician, detaining him. "Let us find the girl first, and bring her to the Lady Barbara. Why agitate her ladyship until the child is found? We must search for her. Every minute counts. We must go to the Black Cottage and compel the Narrs to a confession, and take the girl from them, if they have recaptured "You are right, Sir Graham," cried the baron, arousing himself the dazed and bewildering look deserting his eager, agitated face. "We will hasten to find the—the child. Will you lunch with us?" "I don't mind a bit of refreshment," replied the

doctor. • Lord Champney rang the bell, ordering in a tray of ref resbnients. He then ordered a carriage t- e got ready, with a pair of the fleetest, trestles,. orses. B;; the time Sir Graham had finished the lunch- son the carriage was at the door. The baron was ready, and led the way to the porch. A minute later the two were driving swiftly down the avenue. Half way down the wide drive, Lord Champney put his head out of the carriage and looked back. The Lady Barbara was standing on her balcony, looking after him with a strangely wistful gaze. With a sudden impulse he waved his hat to her, and smiled at her so eagerly that she smiled back. ag tin, and waved her hand. Then, remembering the last night's scene in the drawing-room' the unhappy husband drew back his head with a stifled groan and a ghastly I face. "At least I shall have ore comfort left me," he thought, picturing in his own mind the fair young girl for whom he was now about to search. "My grrotgad child I Her love will be balm to my sorely bruiftd heart." The drive to Chiswick—some fifteen miles—was accomplished in quick time. Lord Cliampney directed his coachman to the Elack Cottage, in Ivy Lane. The cottage had a lonely, deserted look as they drove sip to the high stone wall, and the coachman palled the hell. "Can they have fled ?" asked the ex-minister, uneasily. Before Sir Graham could reply, the old women known as the care-taker of the cottage made her appearance, opening the door in the wall and peer- ing out at them suspiciously. "Are Mr. arid Mrs. Narr at home 2" asked his lordship, mollifying the woman with the gift of a ball-crown. "No, sir, they b'an't," was the response. "They 'ye gone away." "Do you know when they 'II be back '2" "To-day or to-morrow, sir, they expect. ,I am rightirg up the cottage while they 're gone, _and bavir.g bars pat to the windows, which Mrs. Narr war.ts 'ern, on account of her daughter, sir." "Ah I Can you tell us where the Nam have gone 2" Questioned his lordship.

The woman hesitated. The baron drew a gold piece from his pocket and held it up to her. • "Yes," the woman cried, greedity, holding out her hand. "They've gone up the river in a little boat. They went afore daybreak. Their daugh- ter's run away along of a young man, and they've gone after 'em." Lord Champney dropped the coin into the wo- man's hand. After a few more questions, he gave the order to drive on. "What are we to do now, Sir Graham?" he asked, as they went slowly out of the lane. The court physician was looking out of the car- riage, with keen, scrutinizing eyes at a man slouchily dressed, who was lounging on the oorner, looking lazily up and down the lane. "A detective—or I never saw one," said Sir Graham. "A detective in plain clothes. He's on the lookout for some one. -Perhaps for our ami- able friend, Jack Narr. His little forgery business was never settled, you know; and if it's leaked out that he's back in England, that fellow, watch- ing like a lazy old spider there, is after him sure's fate." Lord Champney glanced at the slouchily dressed lounger, and repeated his question. "What are we to do?" echoed Sir Graham, in a puzzled tone. "Bless my soul, if I know. One thing is sure—the Narrs intend to come back when they find the girl. Another thing is equally sure to my mind—they will find her." "I don't see as that is so evident." "Just look at it. The girl escapes at midnight with her lover. No inn will be open to her at that hour, arriving as she does on foot, and unknown. She went in a boat. She'll stay in the boat till morning. By that time some one must have seen her on the river. If she has landed and taken the cars at any station, she will be traced. The Narrs, under the acute villain with them, will certainly find her. They will as certainly bring her back here. If we follow in their track we may lose them. I propose that we go quietly to the lodge arid wait for developments. We can watch from one of my rooms for any arrival at the Black Cottage, and, at the proper rnomont, we can climb over the wall and descend upon them. What do you say, my lord ?" The plan was feasible. Eager and anxious as Lord Charnpney was to follow up Dora, and res- cue her and claim her, he felt that patience and quiet waiting would serve his purpose better than a frantic search. "I will go home with you," he said, sighing. "As you say, we will watch the Black Cottage from your house. lam so impatient, Sir Graham, to see my daughter—for I know this girl is my daughter. And lam almost equally impatient,' he added, his brow darkening, "to be at home again. Heaven only knows what is happening there In my absence!" The new order was given to the coachman, and Champney and Sir Graham were driven to -e.ick Lodge, there to await developments. (To -be eoutinued. )

div.head: RAILWAY SETTLEMENT.
div.p: THE RAILWAY SETTLEMENT.

All the men who were dismissed by the London and 1 North-Western Railway Company resumed work on Mon- day, having been reinstated in their former positions. Mr. Harfordt the general secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants,who returned to London on Monday, stated in an interview that he had advised all the men to go back to work without any ill-feeling, for he did not think they were likely to be marked by the Company, but that,on the contrary, bygones would be bygones. With regard to future action, nothing would be done on behalf ot the men until after the busy season was over,but the men had serious grievances,as the fact that there were shunters working twelve hours a day at dangerous and arduous employment for IBS. 11d, per week clearly showed. Further, there were night shun- tors at Steekport working twelve hours at a stretch witl'ont any time for meals. The men absolutely de- nied the Company's statement to the Board of Trade that the twelve hours included a period of one and a half hours for meals. A man had been suspended for two days for leaving his work to have a meal. The Amal- gamated Society had received many messages of con- gratulation upon the successful issue of the men's pre- ' test. Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., and Ur. H. J. Wil- -1 son,M.P.,had written,and resolutions from labour organ- isations had been numerous. The membership of the Amalgamated Society was likely to be very largely in- creased,judging by the number of applications for enrol- ment forms. Even emergency men employed by the North-Western had applied, and Mr. Harford was con- vinced that in the event of a dispute with the Company these men could be relied on to stand by their felloic- workmen.

WEEKLY CHAT.

The Bimetallic question is occupying the serious considera- tion of the people of the United States of America. The country has passed through the throes of what practically has been a revolution, or an attempt at a revolution. Issues more far-reaching than the Prenela Revolution of the last century have been at stake. Common sense has prevailed. The elec- tion of M`Kinley has dissipated for ever the Bryanire theory that the United States pa, iple were to be caught by a catchy electioneering cry. Trade in Lancashire (although Mr. M'Kin ley perhaps is not the best President that could be elected has received a great impetus, and if Mr M•Kinley will keep his hands off the tariff, trade will continue to increase. Per- haps it is hardly recognised that there is almost as great a revolution taking place at the present time in the Famishing Trade, but this revolution is not in tavonr of unsound money but is in favour of the right's of a man to sell at whatever Price he pleases.

O'er distant hills the rising moon The evening mist dispersed; And, beaming radiant from her throne, She plainly showed my first. A horseman, now seen by her light, Approached with headlong speed; And, as he passed, my second said, To urge his foaming steed. For his lady love still waited, Though the trysting hour was past, My_whole she was, in truth, because He was my third and last. Disc-on-so-late.

A plunge is heard; he will drown, he will sink! He calls for my first. Oh, haste to the brink. A ship at this moment appears in view; My second is there among the crew. The man is saved, and at once cloth exclaim: " Ah, my whole will rejoice to embrace me again, For she's a companion whom ever I find, In joy or in sorrow, most loving and kind. Helpmate

My first is oft a kind of exercise, From which a serious second may arise. My third, to hunt, the prey is in the air. My first again, a mineral, far from rare; My second also means a sort of series; My third sometimes a busy mason wearies. My first is found on every ship that floats; My second, sailors do, in smaller boats. My third is done by peddlers to sell goods. My first-second flees unto the woods, When chased by its enemy, my third, Which the whole names in full; it's a bird. Sparrow hawk.

Industrious's my first I ween, , In households where 'tis often seen; And when the wrong you may pursue, My first you then should quickly do; Second and third ne'er brings success, Nor power does it e'er possess; Homeless and friendless in the street, My total you often chance to meet. Mend-i-cant.

If my first is my second, 'tis sure to be fleet, If my second's my first, it is not fit to eat; And what la my whole will depend upon whether My second and first you fit rightly together. If my second comes first, 'tis an animal; but If my second comes second, why then it is nut. Bo if it's an animal, then i you may back it; But supposing it isn't, I leave you to crack it. Horse-Chestnut.

Here's a man eager for my first; Strange what a most decided thirst Some men have for what is found In this, my *hole. The crackling sound Of second being folded, greets The ear at home and on the streets. Newspaper.

You'll find my first a wild, shrill cry; My whole is often called a hue. My last is never loud nor high, And yet it is to bellow, too. Do my whole you never could; Be my whole you never should.; Wear my whole you often would. _

div.head: GAMES.
div.p: GAMES.

THE BLIND MAN'S CHOICE.—The one who is to pay a forfeit stands with the face to the wall. One behind ,kes signs suitable to a kiss, a pinch, and a box-on-the-ear, and then demands whether the first, second, or third be preferred. Which- ever it chances to be is given. AN AMUSING GAME.—The players are blind- folded in turn, but before the handkerchief is tied over the eyes they are told to look round the room and notice the objects in it, and how they are placed. After being blindfolded they turn round three times, and then say aloud what they expect to touch by walking straight ahead. The mistakes made afford great fun, and if desired forfeits can be paid for each one. Tins Her GAME.—The "hat" is a simple and lively game. The players are divided into two opposing parties. They sit in two half circles at the same distance round a hat, which is placed on the floor in the centre of them. Two differently coloured packs of cards are then given, one to each party, and by them equally dealt out to each player. The players try to throw the cards into the hat in the centre. This is by no means easy. The cards have a way of flying over it or around it in a provoking manner, even when thrown by geed players. The floor is soon littered with failures. The game is played till both packs are exhausted; then those cards which have fallen into the hat are counted, and the side which has the most of its own colour in the hat wins the game.

AMUSING GAME. —Fasten securely a stick two feet long and an inch or more in diameter to the centre of a block of wood or piece of board, so that the block forms a substantial base for the stick, which should be slightly tapered at its upper end. Make out of wire six hoops or rings, three of them nine inches in diameter, two of them seven inches, and one five inches. They 'should be heavy enough to toes easily, perhaps half-an-inch in thickness. Wind these with cloth torn into strips, fastening the ends with needle and thread. Use three colours of the cloth, the rings of each size being the same colour. Red, white and blue makes a pretty combination, using red for the largest size, white for the next, and blue for the one small one. Now set the standard at some distance from the players and the gape begins. One player takes all the rings and tosses them one at a time over the upright stick. For each of the large rings which he succeeds in getting upon the standard, he counts ten; for each of the next size, fifteen; and for the smallest one, twenty-five. Any number agreed upon may be called a game, and the player first obtaining that number of counts wins. After one player has thrown all the rings, another player takes them, tossing them in the same way. Any number of players may take part in the game. When once all round, the first one tosses again, and so on until the game bout. For small children, five or six feet is far enough to toss the rings, bus larger ones may increase the distance. This is also an amusirg game for older persons to try their hand at, and some will probably find out that it requires more dexterity than they imagined to safely land all the rings upon the standard.

div.head: TRICKS AND PUZZLES.
div.p: TRICKS AND PUZZLES.

ESTIMATION OF DIAMETERS. —A threepenny piece, when seen at a short distance from a penny, looks as if it was more than several diameters smaller. Request anyone to guess how many threepenny pieces can be placed fiat upon a penny (one deep only) without the silver coins projecting over the edge of the bronze coin, when tke answer will likely be four, or even five, and great will be the surprise when they find it is impossible to put more than one on the penny, as the diameter of a threepenny piece is more than five-eighths of an inch, and that of a penny under one inch and a quarter. . A GOOD DOMINO TRlCK.—Spread out a set of dominoes upon the table, being careful to extract one for your own use. Inform the company that if they will match the dominoes, you have laid down, using every domino, you will, after leaving the room, determine the numbers at either end of the match. You then leave the room and read the numbers on your stolen domino. This will almost infallibly prove to be the end numbers of the match. When the Match has been formed, and concealed by a handkerchief, you enter the room, and announce the end numbers.

AN INGENIOUS TRICK.—Take a tumbler, and put into it, carefully, a strong syrup of sugar and water, about one-third up the glass. Put on the top of the syrup about the same quantity of milk. They will not mix if this be done carefully, the milk floating on the surface of the syrup • on the surface of the milk pour some wine, which, in its turn, will float and not Mix. Thus you have three different•liquids in one glass, totally separate from each other. You may undertake to drink anyone of •them without disturbing the rest, and perform this apparently impossible feat by taking a straw, putting it carefully into the syrup, milk, or wine, and drawing up the liquor through it. THE PENETRATIVE PENNY.—In a piece of stout paper cut a circular hole the size of a shilling— i.e., about one-sixteenth less than an inch. Invite anyone to pass a penny through the hole without touchino• the coin or tearing the paper. He will naturally tell you that it can't be done, the diameter of a penny being one inch and a quarter, or five-sixteeenths of an inch larger than the hole, and yet the thing can be done, easily done. Fold the paper exactly across the centre of the hole; then take it in both hands and ask some One to drop the penny into the fold, let it rest just over the hole, the lower edge projecting below. Bend the • corners of the papers slightly upwards. This elongates the opening, and, if the movement be continued, the penny will, after a second or two, fall through by force of its own weight. The paper remains uninjured. A Cunious EXPERIMENT. —lf you put a silver spoon above the flame of a candle, it becomes black; plunge it into a glass of watar—what a change! The spoon is no longer black. Take it from the water, you will think the smoke has disappeared; it is not so; the spoon remains of a beautiful dull black. Curious sit not? The explanation is simple. Lamp black,i because of its fineness, is not made wet by the water; the water presents then, all round and at a distance from the blackened spoon, a curved form reproducing exactly that of the spoon, and on which the light reflects as on a metallic surface. Try this pretty experiment this way. Blacken an egg above a candle or, better still, a very smoky lamp, and this egg, plunged into the water, will take instantly a brilliant and metallic aspect, giving the illusion of a silvered egg, and reappearing black as soon as you take it out of the water. To RUB ONE SIXPENCE INTO Two.—Wet a six- pence slightly, and stick it to the under edge of a table (without ,a cover) at the place where you are sitting. Then borrow a sixpence from one of the company; tuck up your sleeves and open your fingers to show that you have not another coin concealed about you, and commence rubbing, it backwards and forwards on the table with your right hand, holditig your left hand under the edge of the table to catch it. After two or three pre- tended unsuccessful attempts to accomplish your object, loosen the sixpence under the table with the tips of the fingers of your left hand, just when you are sweeping the borrowed sixpence into it. Rub them for a little while together in your hands, and then throw them on the table to the amaze- ment of the audience.

A TRICK Fon THE Boys.—Here is a good trick that one boy played on another, and perhaps you can get some fun out of it. Jim and John were talking together, when Jim took a piece of chalk out of his pocket, and said: "I tell you what, I can draw a ring around you with this piece of chalk and you can't get out of it without taking off your hat." "You can't do it !" said John. "I can," replied Jim. "Well, let's see you do it." "You'll have to shut your eyes." "All right." So John shut his ey, - while Jim walked around him, pretending to IN. inaking a mark on the floor. " There !" he "Where is the ring?" said John, opening his eyes and looking around. "On your hat !" said John. "Let's see you get out of it without taking your hat off." John looked at his hat, and sure enough there was a ring chalked around the brim.

Ir half the Somalis die, what will the other half do 7—Go blackburying. WHY is a clock like a collier 7—Because he goes on tick while on the strike.
WHAT come after meat on Christmas Day ? Pudding. And what comes after cheese ?—Mice. WHAT went to India and stopped there, and yet came back because it never went there 7—A watch.
WILY cannot a tall gentleman legally possess a short walking-stick ?—Because it can never belong to him.
WHAT is the longest wprd in the English lan- guage ?--Smiles, because there is a mile between the first and last letters.

'WHAT is the difference between a mare and an egg 7—One is an egg (he gee gee) and the other is a she gee gee. WHY are tears like potatoes 7—Because they, spring from the eyes. WHICH travels the faster—heat or cold 7—Heat, of course; anybody can catch cold. WHY are jokes like nuts 7—Because the drier they are the better they crack. ' WHY is a horse like a sugar-plum 7—Because the more you lick it the faster it goes.

WHAT people did Crusoe first meet on the desert island 7—A great swell running up the beach, and a little cove running inland. WHICH two animals took the least luggage into the ark 7—The cock and the fox, who had only a brush and comb between them.

WHY are railway companies like laundressev ? Because they have ironed the whole country, ,and sometimes,do a little mangling. Wiri does a cabman consider it a fine day when it rains hard? Because he considers it fare-weather. , _ _
WHY is a pig in a parlour like a house on fire ? Because the sooner it is put out the better. WHY is a person who never lays a wager as bad as a regular gambler ?—Because he is no better.
WHY is a man clearing a hedge in a single jump like a man snoring ?—Because he does it in his leap I (his sleep).

There is much comment upon the dramatic union of all parties in Ireland which is taking place under the influence of the agitation for a reform of. the financial relations between Great Britain and the sister island. To find "Loyalists "and Nationalists, Catholics and Protestants, all joining together on the same platforms for a,common national purpose excites no surprise in Liberal quarters, but is a most comforting confirmation of the views they have been expressing for years, and which were the foundation of the Home Rule Bill. It is pointed out that it reduces to its true proportions the thea- trical demonstrations of terror and undying hatred of their fellow-countrymen with which the Ulster Brigade has deluged the English Unionists. The English Unionists here are very,angry. It is they, probably, who will suffer most loss of prestige by this demonstration of the possibility of all parties in Ireland living and working together. a

The Princess of Wales remains tho whole of this week in London, when she will purchase !ler Christmas gifts, a matter that the Princess always carries out herself at this season. The Prince and Princess will proceed to Sandringham on Saturday for Christmas.

rhe Board of Trade report issued on Monday shows that the labour market continues to im- prove. There are fewer unemployed men than for some years past, and from all parts of the coubtry and nearly all• trades there are reports of more work and better wages. The unorganised agricul- tural labourers—the men employed in the largest industry in the country—are the most important section of those who do not bane& by revival or improvement in trade. Tbe better prices obtained for agricultural produce during the last few months.and the large subsidies under the Rating Bill seem all to go to the employer and landlord, whilst the labourer, without a trades union, still pursues his hopeless journey down hill, with the workhouse at the bottom.

I understand that .the arrangements for the transfer of the "Sun," Mr. T. P. O'Connor's daily paper, to its new Tory proprietori are now practi- cally complete. The paper will be taken over on Saturday, and will at once commence its new life under new proprietors, a new editor, and with a new political creed. In future it will be Tory- Democratic, whatever that may mean, and once more the "Star" and the "Westminster Gazette" will be left alone to represent Liberalism in the London evening Press, with more than half a dozen competitors. The "Pall Mall Gazette," which tried to maintain an independent attitu le, is falling more and more under the deraivation of the Tory party in general politics, and that wretched section of it which labels itself 'Moderate" in metropolitan municipal affairs.

A statement is made that a syndicate of English capitalists have obtained a concession for the con- struction of a hang railway in China which will give Great Britain some considerable compensation for the supposed privileges acquired by Russia un- der the alleged treaty which was announced last week. The existence of the t ussian treaty still lacks consolation, and the Foreign Office denies all knowledge of the alleged English railway. It is, however,known here that the effort which has been made pretty continuously for many years to per- suade the Chinese authorities to allow the country to be opened up by British capital have been strongly reinforced during recent months by a special expedition from London. It is now believed that success has crowned their efforts.

I understand that Mr. Earnest T. Hooley, the donor of a communion set of pure gold to St. Paul's Cathedral has been elected a member of the Pociety for Promoting Christian Knowledge. This institution is probably the oldest missionary society in the Anglican Church, having been founded in 1698. People who know it chiefly, as an enterpris- ing publishing house can have but a small idea of its many-sided activities. It was once said by a distinguished dignitary of the Church that it was nnly by the work of the S.P.C.K..at home that the Church was able to carry on her work abroad. The gocietv makes grants varying from £35,000 to .£40,000 every year for church building in the colonies, for medical missions, for the spiritual care of emigrants, and for other Chnrch purposes in all parts of the world. The Society is, however, in ureat need of support, the exnenditure exceeding the income last year by £20,000.

The inquiry into the so-called scandals of the County Council Works Department was opened on Wednesday afternoon at the County Hall by Sir A. Arnold, assisted by eight members of the Council and two " outside " assessors, Mr. Edwin Water- house and Mr. Gruner. Befere the proceedings commenced members were furnished with a lengthy statement prepared by Mr. Binnie, the Council's engineer, who, having no administrative connection with the Works Department, may be taken as an unbiassed witness. Mr. Einnie's statement was one long eulogy of the department, which, he said, had executed work just as well as an outside contractor and, so far as he had been able to judge, at lower prices. In his spoken evidence the engineer repeated this strong testimony, and added that if the department were continued on proper lines he could conceive that the quality of the work might excel that done by contractors without any addi- tional cost to the Council. He made the provifo, however, that there must be greater co-operation than hitherto between the various departments concerned in the undertaking.

SIR S. T. BRUNNER; M.P., ON UNDENOAIIN&TIONAL EDUCA.TION.

1 On Saturday afternoon Sir John Brunner, M.P., opened a new Congregational day school at Lower Dar- wen, near Blackburn, which has taken the place of a Church of England school.—Sir John said he was there to participate in the celebration of a victory in the great cause of unsectarian education. Such victories were usually the result of a bitter sectarian confict, but in this case he wished them to regard it as a victory for principle and for Christianity as distinguished from creed. In contending for undenominational teaching in elementary day schools, he said that that sort of educa- tion was the education which they considered alone fit for children of tender years. In day schools, little children ought to be instructed only in those religious truths upon which all Christians were agreed. The ChurTh of Eneland taught theolog,ical dogmas in their schools, and this was a gre.-.c mistake, for the less dogmatic the teaching children received the better Christians they would grow up in after life. The sooner the Church of England realized this fact, the sooner would she right herself among the educational institutions of this country. Referring to the educa- tional differences they wens experiencing at North wich, he saki i resolved itself into a fight between the Bishop of Chester and himself. The Bishop had threa- tened to build a Church of England school, and he (Sir John Brunner) had replied that, in that event, he would build an undenomina.tional school, and back its success against that of the Bishop's establishment. The fight, however, had net yet extended beyoni private corres- pondence between hims3lf and the Bi3hop, and the best of feeling was maintained up to the present. He an- ticipated a mutually satisfactory settlement of the difficulty.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD LOCKS.
div.p: THE FATAL ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD LOCKS.

Mr. S. Brighouse conducted an inquiry in the Parade Room, Irlarn-st., on Monday afternoon relative to the death of William Rowe, an able-bodied seaman on the ship Cragg, who met with injuries at Latchford locks which resulted in his death at the Warrington Infirmary- on Friday night. Mr. Robert O'Berry appeared on be- half of Messrs. Fisher, Renwick and Co., owners of the venel, and Captain Waring, superintendent ef the War- rington section of the canal, was also present.—Annie Rowe was the first witness called, and deposed that the deceased was her brother. AO WAS a native of New- castle, and was almost coritinually on board his vessel. Be was 18 years et age last birthday, and she last saw him alive about six weeks ago. She saw him the previ- ous day lying dead at the Infirmary.—George Brown, pier-master at Latchford locks, stated that the steamship Craeg entered the 651 t. lock at Latchford at ten o'clock on Friday morning. The vessel was going down the canal from Manchester. .The vessel had very little weigh. The deceased was astern, paying out a wire- rope for the purpose of securing the vessel in the lock when by some means the deceased must have stepped into a coil and his leg suddenly become fast. Witness saw what had happened and shouted to the captain"full speed astern," but before this could be done the rope tightened round the deceased's leg, and he was dragged against the bulwarks and thrown into the lock. The deceased was got out of the lock as speedily as Possible, and conveyed to the Warrington Infirmary. Everything that could be done for toe man was done by the captain of the vessel.—F. Nicho- las, lockezate man at Latchford locks, stated that lie took the stern rope of the vessel Cragg when she came into the lock and put it over a" mushroom." He then went to close the lock gates, and whilst doing so he heard a shout from the ship. He at once saw something was wren., the deceased being entangled in a coil of wire rope. Witness ran to the mushroom" and endeavoered to take the rope off, but by the time he got there the rope had become taut,and he could not remove it. Rowe was drawn to the side of the bulwarks and afterwards thrown overboard. Ile was of the opinion that the man must have stepped into the coil of rope accidentally, and it fastened his kg. before he could extricate himself. If the deceased had had the presence of mind to jump overboard he would not have receivel the injuries to the leg as the rope could not then have become taut.—Nurs • Dobson said the deceased was admhted into the Warrington Infirmary about 11.50 on Friday morning suffering from severe injuries to the right leg which exrendeefrem above the knee to the hip.- El" was in a state of cellapse the whole time. He asked witn-ss to tell his sister that it was quite an acci- dent.—The Coroner remarked that he was very pleased with the conduct of the captain rf the vessel in looking after the man as he did.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

ORA.PPENHA.LL.

The sheet almanac which we present to our readers to-day, contains, as will be seen, a photo- graphic view of Grappenhall. With this village all Warrington people are more or less famliar. It is pleasantly situated and has a quiet, old-world air about it. Amid the changing scenes of both town and country. on all hands, the village of Grappenhall continues comparatively unaffected. It affords, in this respect, a striking contrast with many of the neighbouring parishes. Latchford, which formerly formed part of Grappenhall has been transformed by the Manchester ship Canal and the London and North-Western Railway, and quite recently a large portion of it has been in- cluded in the borough. Appleton is likewise undergoing a great change, and is more and more becoming a large suburb of Wszrington, brought into constant touch with the town by an omnibus service. But Grappenhall,as we have said,remains comparatively untouched by modern enterprise. There is the same village street with the parish church and its prominent tower at its head, and if no assembly of freemen any longer meets on the village green, the space in front of the chnrch is still there,partly occupied by the village inn. Near too, the stocks are to be seen in good preservation; but no longer used for the punishment of petty offenders.

Although Grappenhall is without a published history, it lias a history nevertheless. The origin of the name of the village is pro- bably derived from grappe—a bunch of grapes— which in the plural would be grappen. The earliest notice of the place is in Domesday (1086) from which we gather that Osbern (Fitz lezzon) ancestor of the Boydels held " Gropenhale," and its two freemen, Edward and Dot, held it as two manors, Latchford probably being one. It is also very probable that when Grappenhall first became a parish it was taken out of Lymm, Osbern Fitz Tezzon being lord paramount of that place in addi- tion to Grappenhall. For many generations the Boydel family retained its position of consequence as owners of Grappenhall but the village seems to have been afterwards given to William Fitz Sam- son, who about the time of Richard I. re-leased it to Hugh de Boydel. The deed transferring it to him is rather an interesting document, and runs as fol- lows :—" Be it known to all men that I, William Fitz Samson, for my defect of service, have given and wholly released to my Lord de Boydel, Gropen- hale, with all its appurtenances in wood and in plain, the half of three parts of a knight's fee, only excepted, for which gift my lord the said Hugh de Boydel hath given me three marks, in presence of Ralph de Mainwaringe, justice of Chester, Hamon de Many, and others." This same Hugh Boydel it may be mentioned obtained a grant from the Earl of Chester (Randle Blundeville) in the reign of Richard I: of a free passage along the river Mersey between Runcorn and Thel- wall. Sir John Boydel became thee heir ilof the possessions which ultimately fell into the hande of is second zen. Robert Boydel, of Caterich, in "Gropenhale," who had that piece by the gift of his father in the reign of Richard 111. (1337). Cate- rich still retains some ancient memorials of its old possessors. Redish Hall, where they had a seat for a considerable time, has some fine oak panellings of the time of James 1, with some curious old beams in the roof. To-day it is used as a farmhouse, and has undergone a great change. The Boydel name seems to have become extinet at Grappenhail on the death of Robert Boydel who died in the reign of Henry IV., 1406, without issue. There were, how- ever, two of his sisters left, one of whom was Mar- garet, the wife of Hugh Redish, and she became the possessor of the lands in Grappenhall. Thomas Redish, her descendant, came into possession on her death in 1447. In 1556, the na,ues of the proprietor of Grappenhall agaio changes, in consequence of the marriage of Maud, the heiress of Thomas Redish. of iJatericli, with William Marbury. The oc,ceapier of Redish Hall in 1653, according to a register of a servant's burial, was Peter Brooke, the member for Newton, in the Long Parliament. Togive anything like a full achount of the parish church would occupy more of our space than we can give. But it may be stated that the church, like those at Mebberley, Chorley and Halton, is dedicated to St. Wilfrid as its patron saint. The festival of St. Wilfrid is set down in the calendar as occurring on the 12th October, and Grappenhall wakes, which are now a thing of the past,were kept on the last Sunday of that month, but the orienta- tion of the church seems to have been on the 15th April, or the 29th August, 1539, and therefore has no connection with the then auspicious celebration of,Ae sakes. These dates must not be taken as those of the foundation of the church, for evidence seems to point to the fact that the early part of the twelfth century was the date of the foundation of the original parish church at Grappenhall. It fie! possible that the parish chest,of a very rude design, now in the Museum at Warrington, also belougs tol this period. The church as i; stande today, has little to recommend itself architectural:ly. It is a sample of 16th century work, and ma:, most promi- nent feature of it is the tower. The cat-like animal carved on the string coterie of the tower is probably a pun,perpetrated in stone on the name of Caterich where the Boydels, or their successors had their seat, or it may be, as had been suggested, the crest of some neighbouring landowner, who gave liberally:towards the building of the tower, or the device of the architect or mason. The present rector of the parish is the Rev. Richard Greenall, M.A , nephew of tne late Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., who was the pe'sron of the living. The sun dial to be found near the church was set up in 1747,but a still more ancient memorial of the past is the venerable yew tree, which counts its years by the century. In rambling through the churchyard one comes across many noteworthy monuments and epitaphs. Some of the dates carry you back to the 16th and 17th centuries. A thym- ing epitaph is a rarity but here is one to be seen referring to the Longshays family—a narise still familar in Warrington and district, and that of a family which occupied Redish Hall at one time :

" John Longshaw, of Latchford. was buried here, Nineteenth of August in the year, 176 aged 68. Christian, his wife, did before him die, And here below their bodies lie, August 21, 1761, aged 61. William, their son, was called away, Interred hers on the igh h day, December 1776, .ged 27. Another son, John was his name, Soon after his brotivr hither came.
ugust 29. 1776, aged 27. Sarah, wife of William Gregson, Departed this life march 27, 1804, aged 72 A loving wife, a mother clear, A. faithfui friend I've burled here,
Who lived In love and died in peace, I hope her joys will never cease."
NERAL NEWS.

Dr. T. Thorne, chief medical officer of the British Local Government Board, accompanied by a colleague, has arrived in Brussels to study the vaccination system in Belgium, and the laws and regulations beating upon the subject. An interesting historical document has fund its way into a London auction mart, and will (says the "Chronicle") shortly be put up for sale. It is the warrant, signed by Sir Francis Drake, Sir John Haw- kins, and Lord Burghley, ordering certain Bristol mer- chants tc be paid for ships supplied against- the Spanish Armada and dated October 1, 1588. It is a little torn at the top, but the signatures are unNjured.

From a statement Made on Tuesday.: to a press repre- sentative, it appears that Mr. Ernest Honley and those associated with him in the purchase of Trafford Park have been for several mOnthr. past closely engaged on plans for the development ci the estate. Soon after the Christmas holidays Mr. Marshall Stevens will be in the active seryice of the syndicate. Works on a large scale, which are to give employment to a large number of hands, will he begun next year. A Chicago paper, under the heading " Victoria: Sixty Years a Queen," makes the suggestion that the 18th Highlanders of the Canadian Militia forces should be invited to Chicago to join the British-American organi- sations there in a celebration of the anniversary of the Queen's accession. This is," it adds, " a reciprocal a-r for the magnificent welcome given by the Queen, a Wales.and people of Britain to the Hon Artillery Com- pany this year."

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

HOCKEY MATCH.—PERKETH PARK V. ALTRINCHAAI. Played at Penketh on Saturday. The visitors were with- out a goalkeeper, while the home team had their full strength. From the opening bully Altrincham pressed,the home custodian being beaten three times by brilliant shots from the stick of B.Brewer. Shortly after half-time Brewer had to retire hurt, and -tie visitors were left with nine men only ; but in spite of this Advantage the home teak were unable to notch a point. Close on time Stanler shot a good goal I 7 the visitors, hut as the home referee did not see it, and their were no nets, it vvAs disallowed. Nothing further was scored, and when no side was called Altrincham retired winners of a very unpleasant game by three goals to love.

div.head: EXNMINEIi.
div.p: THE EXNMINEIi.
FRIDAY, DECEMBER I.Btb, 1896.

THE Armenian atrocities and file National Liberal education question were the chief Federation. , subjects under discussion at the meeting of the General Committee of the National Liberal Federation held at Liverpool on Wednesday. Both of these subjects are likely to figure pretty prominently during the next session of Parliament. The resolution that was adopted with reference to Armenia probably expresses with a fair degree of accuracy the feelings of the Liberal party throughout tho country. It does not condemn the Government for its policy in deal- ing with the SULI7A.N, nor does it express approval of that policy. As a matter of fact, the country has, in connection with the latest developments of the Eastern question, been kept in the dark to an almost unprecedented extent. Apparently no- body, with the exception of Lord SALISBURY him- self, can say what has been done for the purpose of protecting the remnants of the Armenian people from utter extermination. It is believed that Lord SAusennY has applied himself to the accom- plishment of that object,though with what succese or want of success no one can definitely say. So far as can be judged from outward appearance, the Sultan is still master of the situation, and the world may at any time be startled by massacres as bad or even worse than those which have already been recorded. It is true that every now and again vague statements gre published to the effect that the "great powers," or, at all events, Russia, Franee, and Great Britain, have agreed to take combined action; but days and weeks pass by and nothing is done. This, of coorse, may not be Lord SALISBURY'S fault; in fact most people in this country are very willing to be- lieve that it is not his fault. At the same time there is not sufficient evidence at hand upon Which any approval of his line of policy can be based. "Under these circumstances the resolution passed at Liverpool is probably as judiciously wordedto any I 'solution could be under the cir- cumstances. It reads as follows That this com- mittee, recognising the importance of joint action by the Penn of Europe for the better govern- ment of therViirkish Empire and the prctection of Its Christian subjects expresses its profound re- gret that the attempts which have been made up to the present time to bring about such action have been so barren of good result. The commit- tee notes with satisfaction the abandonment by Lord SALISIURY of the false policy which he and Lord BEACONSFIELD adopted,of assuming a neces- sary antagonism between Great Britain and Russia, and hopes that the Ministerial explana- tions to Parliament will prove that the old policy of supporting the Turkish Empire is now at an end; but the committee places on record its belief that the nation will hold the Government guilty unless it proves beyond question that every effort has been made, and is still being made, to give effect to the views which the country has expre7scd at public meetings marked by such extraordinary spontaneity and absence of party feeling." That, as we have said. appears to be a reasonable posi- t-on to tskenp under the circumstances of the moment, but it is about time that our Foreign Secretary and Prime Minister gave tL, eountry at large more information than he has yet condes-

conded to impart. After all, this is the country's business and not simply one of Lord SALISBURY'S private affairs. The English people as a whole are prepared to admit that the persecuted Armenians have a real and serious claim upon them, and they are prepared to meet that claim in every reason- able way. In spite of what is said in German newspapers there is no desire in this country to bring about a European war,qbut short of provok- ing that calamity, Lord SALISBURY has, practi- cally, had a free hand. How has he used his opportunity P He gives no answer to that ques- tion himself, but we believe that the Liberal party may be relied upon to insist upon an answer being given to Parliament. Upon the education question a much more de- finite note was struck. The Committee urges upon the Liberal associations of the country "the duty of again resisting to the uttermost any attempt Which the present Government may mitke to re- vive sectarian controversy and religious inequality under the guise of educational reform, and of in- sisting that all elomentary schools, whether board et voluntary, shall be treated alike in any further grants of money from the State; that the provi- sion of public money for the educational purposes shall be accompanied by an adequate measure of local representative control; that nothing shall be Permitted to injure the school board system, which has worked for 25 years with conspicuous success; and that further grants to the voluntary schools shall be ace mapanied by some guarantee that the money will be expended in promoting efficiency and raising the standard of education, and not in elieving the subscribers to those schools of their Present financial obligations." The Committee also repeated its opinion that the demands of the tsachers in voluntary Fchools for relief from corn-
Pilsory extraneous duties and for reasonable
_ eeenrity of tenure ought to be granted. , We notice that the most important of all points ln Connection with this controversy was kept well

to the front in the discussion on the resolution— that is to say, the general efficiency of education. Whatever may be said about the various claims of denominationalists or undenominatibnalists, as such, this country simply cannot afford to have its edncation degraded or rendered less efficient to please any section or party. That is the condi- tion which dominates all others in this question. If the English are to hold their place as a great industrial and progressive nation they will in the future not have to be worse educated than they • are now, but better. An efficient national ed uca- tion is only to be had by the !free expenditure of money, and if the Government should prove to be so il-advised as to attempt to lessen the monetary resources of the School Boards or other public educational authorities in order to conciliate sec- tarianism of any kind it will again find that it bas seriously miscalculated the national temper.

EAUTHQUAKES are fortunately of The Earthquake. very rare occurrence in this country, " but there is now no doubt that one did happen on Thursday. It was a Very little earthquake when placed in com- parison with the seismic disturbances that occur in other parts of the world—in "Far Japan" for instance—but its authenticity is. attested by evi- dence from many different quarters. It was dis- tinctly Celt in Warrington, and more particularly it would seem in the Latchford district of the borough. But its effects were not confined to this immediate locality, for it was,felt over a large por- tion of England and Wales. At Birmingham this alarming tremor of Mother Earth must have been very noticeable for it is reported that in the Mid land capital many people were so frightened that they ran out of their houses in their night-clothes. At Hereford the results were serious and deplor- able. One poor woman was so 'overcome by the lifting and 'rocking of her house that she died from fright, and even men were thoroughly unnerved by the strange movement of the earth P In fact, the earthquake seems to have been more severely felt at Hereford than in any other part of the country, as it was there violent enough to throw down a church pinnacle and to damage many buildings. A writer from Ince Blundell, which is, of course, much nearer home than either Birmingham or Hereford, gives a vivid account of the shock. He says that "at 5.5 a.m. I was awakened by hearing loud bellowing from the shippon and the barking of all the doge. The next instant I heard aloud crash, lour windows on the first floor being smashed into thousands of pieces. The walls of the house trembled perceptibly and the bedroom furniture seemed to move. At.the tirne the wind was blow- ing very strong, accompanied by remarkably vivid flashes of lightning. Such a night I never re- member. The loud rumblingnoise will never fade from my memory." All these reports are very disquieting no doubt, but after all there is no cause for the panic which, it is said, prevails in some quarters. Although earthquakes have been few and far between in this count 7, this is not by any means the first of its kind. Similar pheno- mena have been experienced in the past and have done little or no damage beyond scaring a num- ber of people. In spite of certain predictions to the contrary the chances are that there will be no repetition of the present disturbances.

Those of our readers who have perused that much talked of book " Made in Germany" will pro- bably remember that the author has some deprecia- tory remarks with reference to the British soap trade. He asks " Why should this manufacture be so largely in foreign hands? They twit Us with our debased fondness for the tub, and they t o but add injury, to insult when they send us the soap for use therein. The Germans—a non-tubbing race— have not as yet invaded the English soap market so victoriously as is their wont; though even here the Teuton hand may be discerned by the expert in forged trade-marks. At. present their chief success —complete in its way—in the soap trade consists in routing the English export by means of protec- tive duties, and this they have effectually accom- plished. One very big English firm has tried to break the bkrier down. But that English firm has failed, for the German genius loves not reciproc- ity." It will be noted that the writer gives no statistics to prove that the manufacture of soap is in foreign hands, as he would have us believe.

In his able reply to "Made in Germany," Mr George W. Medley, to whose book entitled "The German Bogey," we referred last week, knocks the bottom out of the argument—such as it is with reference to soap. Mr. Medley says :—"lf we begin with 1866, when our soap export wai of the value of £241,109 with the price 27•48s.per cwt., and cast our glance through the intervening years down to 1895, when our export amounted to £756,704, the price being 20785.. per cwt., there is not a single year in which there was any near approach to our last year's trade." Judging by the healthy state of the soap trade in this district, we cannot believe that the " routing " referred to by 'he author of " Made in Germany" is having the eneic' he wishes us to believe on our export trade.
