*** CII6ItTMAS DAY,—Atil Christmas Day falls upon Friday next week the" Examiner "will be published on Thursday.
DEATH OF MRS. GERRARD, RUNCORN.

On Friday,Mrs. Elizabeth Gerrard, aged 75 years, died at her residence, 27, Waterloe-road, after a long illness. Her husband, tho late Mr. Charles Garrard, was for- merly well-known in the town and district. At one time he was proprietor of the" Warrington Standard" published in that town, but subsequently ( ime to Run- corn. He was a past master of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons. As well as the Widnes Lodge. Mrs. Gerrard leaves crie son and three daughters (one of whom is in America) to mourn her loss. The interment took place on Tuesday at the WArrington cemetrry.
HEAVY SENTENCE ON A-RUNCORN GREENGROCER.

Frederick Chell was charged at the Runcorn Polite Court on Tuesday morning with being drunk and disor- derly and assaulting P.C. Nicholls in High-street on the previous day. Sergeant Lee and P.C. Nicholls having given evidence, Chelt was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour for being drunk, and 6 weeks' hard labour for the assault. VOLUNTIMR NIGIT MAUCH.

The Runcorn detachment of the 2nd Battalion of Earl of Chester's Volunteers are having the last night march of the season en Saturday night. 'the Runcorn corps will assemble at the Drill Shed and then proceed by train to Frodsham, where they will be met by the Frods.ham and Elartford corps. The Companies will then march to Dunham Hill and back, a distance of five miles each way.

The Runcorn Library Committee held their monthly meeting op Tuesday in the Council Chamber. Mr. Han- kinson presided. The statement of accounts showed that there was a balance of £57 lls. 7d. after paying all expenses. The Librarian (Mr. J. D. div.head: SCALDING FATALITY AT RUNCORN:
div.p: SCALDING FATALITY AT RUNCORN:

John Patrick Reche, aged eight months, on of Patrick Roche, 3 Heath-road, Runcorn, died on Wednesday from scalds received on the 13th inst. The child was at home on Sunday last when some het ligoid was spilt upon him. He was severely scalded about the body, and died as above stated. CAMDEN FOREIGN MISSION SOCIETY.

On behalf of the mission cause, special sermons w ere preached in the Camden Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday, by Ms. Spivy of Widnes and the Rev. T. Brackenberry. On Monday the annual meeting was held in the church, Mr. P. Speakman, J.P., C. Aid., presided, and was sup- ported by the Revs. W. George aud R. J. Clifton. Mr. A. Harrison and Mr. J. Barley. The Rev. E. Homer Pear son,of Liverpool,was present as the deputation from the parent society and gave a most effective address on the success already accomplished by the missionaries, and showed that the out-look of the society was full of hope. The report read by Mr. Naylor the local secretary showed that thb young people and the Sunday school scholars had worked vary earnestly during the year on behalf of the society. The Rev. R. J. Clifton then de- livered an impressive address. Votes of thanks were passed and the meeting terminated. RUNCORN UNIONISTS AND THE LATE MR. Jonar BRUNDRIT.

On Friday evening, at a meeting of Unionists, under the presidency of Mr. J. J. Speakman, the following re- solution was unanimously passed, in the motion of the Chdirrnah.seconded ley Mr. Summerfield, and supported by Messrs. J. K. Digges,J. W. Lightburn, LP., A. Light- burn and others :—" That this meeting,in passing a vote of condolence with the family of the late J. Brundrit, Esq., J.P., in their sad bereavement, desires to express its deep sense of the unwearied and invaluable services rendered by him as leader of the Conservative party in tills town, and the meeting further deplores the irrepar- able loss the "Unionist party has sustained by his lament- able death." THE NEW THEATRE FOR RUNCORN.

On Saturday afternoon several members of the thea- trical profession assembled at Lowlands-road for the purpose of witnessing the laying of the foundation stone for the new theatre. Amongst those present were Mr. and Mrs. Caddick, Mr. A. C. Percy, Mr. S. Davies, and Mr. W. Farrell. Mrs. Caddick declared the stone well and truly laid. (Applause.) She asked to be allowed on behalf of her husband and herself to express their gratitude and return their most sincere thanks for the kindness showed to them during their stay of seven years in Runcorn. She hoped the prosperity of the new theatre would be the same as the old one. In conclu- sion, she wished prosperity to the town of Runcorn. (Loud applause.) Mr. S. Davies then presented to Mrs. Caddick a ',liver trowel. The fallowing is a description of the building. The theatre will be plainly but sub- stantially erected ef bricks with stone and terra-cotta dressings sparingly introduced. The roof will be of red tiles. The entrance ball, will be 55 feet by 12 feet, the auditorium 65 feet by 47 feet, and the stage 50 feet by 30 feet. The clear height of the stage portion will be 40 feet from the level of the stage to the underside the "grid," thus giving every facility for the manipulation of the scenery without rolling. Above the" grid" easy access will be arranged to all parts of the stage. The proscenium will be 25 feet wide and 20 feet :high. In addition to the scene dock,store rooms, heating chamber manager's office, and retiring room for the orchestra there will be provision for twelve airy and well lighted dressing-rooms. All the staircases will be of stene,there will be ample emergency exits, the doors will open out- wards, fire hydrants will be placed in convenient posi- tions, and every provision made for the safety ard comfort of the public The contractors for the work are Messrs. William Farrell and Son, of South etank,Runcorn and the architect is Mr. Samuel Davies, lf Devonshire Buildings, Runcorn and Fredsham,under whose personal supervision the building will be erected. The theatre will accommodate about 2,000 people. PAIMITITH METIODIST CIRAPIL, RUNCORN.

div.head: SALE OF WORK.
div.p: SALE OF WORK.

On Saturday afternoon a sale of work was held in the Newtown School, Runcorn, for the purpose of raising money to carry out necessary rerairs to St. Michael's Churcb,and also to start a fund for the ptovision of an organ. There were several stalls laden with a variety of choice articles,and a good company assembled at the opening ceremony,araongst those present being the Rev. Canon and Mrs. Maitland Wood,the Revs. H. C. Moyle, W. Scholes,atid W. H. Stubbs,Mrs. and Miss Preston,Mr. and Mrs. C. H. R. Harrison, Mrs. Reacher, Miss Smith, Mrs. and Miss Crosby, Mrs. Imison, Mrs. and Miss Abel, Mrs. Weston, Miss Dalloway, Mr. and Miss Mellor, M. 3 Moyle,and Mr. C. Pownall. Miss Barclay bad been an- nounced to perform the opening cerensopy, but was un- able to fulfil the engagement, and Mr. W. Mellor intro- duced Mrs. Maitland Wood to perform the duty.

The Rev. Canon Wood said be reed not refer to the sad circumstances 'which. bad prevented Miss Barclay being present, beyond saying they all sympathised very much with the family in their very great loss, which they would feel for a long time to come. At the same time they regretted Miss Barclay's absence because of the sad re,ason,and because they would lose considerable help in consequence. Alluding to the object of the sale, t e Vicar said they had a very beautiful church -inside, and when it was finished, a very noble church on tha outside, but when they had seen that they bad seen everything. There was absolurely nothing, at all in the way of money or anything else which enabled that church to go on except what was given. This,of course was a thing they could not lay too much stress upon because the people of the Church of England were very much apt to depend upon endowments and the exer tions of their ancestors, but in this case there was abso- lutely nothing at all. Mrs. Wood then declared the sale open. Mr. Mellor proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Wood for performing the ceremony, and to the Vicar for his very able speech. The Rev. C. H. Moyle seconded the motion, remarking upon Mrs. Wood's goodness in taking Miss Barclay's place at very short notice. The sale then proceeded, the list of stalls and stall- holders being :—Working rarty Stall, Mrs. Heap, Mrs. Melloy, Miss Moyle. Mrs. Povvnall. Pottery Stall, Mrs. Dunning. Refrzshment Stall, Mrs. C. Harrison,Mrs. A. Lightburn, Mrs. Miles, Mrs. J. Speakman, Miss Stubbs, and Mrs. Ridge. Bran Tub, Miss E. Miles, Miss H. Poemall. Miss E. Roberts, Miss B. Mellor, Miss C. Price, Master W. Dunning, and others also assisted. • The amount received was £s2—a result which must be very satisfactory to all concerned, and especially to the members of the sewing party, who for many months have been assiduously working to gain such a euccess. Various entertainments were given in the afternoon and evening.

div.head: EARTHQUAKE.
div.p: THE EARTHQUAKE.
THE SHOCK FELT AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday night and Weonesday morn ing frost visited Runcorn and district. The streets were like sheets of ice, and were only with difficulty traversed. About noon it commenced to thaw, and at night to all appearances it was thought likely to freeze again. had it done so, the streets would have been impassable. On Wednesday night and yesterday naorning ( l'hursday) the atmospheric conditlons changed and snow fell heavily. During the morning about 5-30 a.m. a curious rumbling noise was baud. Of course this surprised many of the inhabitants who were slumbering and some of them got up to see if an explosion had taken place near their dwellings. The shock was zo severe that many beds and articles of furniture were rocked with the vibration. Though people were alarmed they did not at first realise what the shock was. Mr. Bock, chemist, Bridge-street, was awakened by the shock at 5-30 by what he supposed to be as earthquake shock. Hie bed rocked by the vibra- tion. Mr. Mellor, grccer, High-street, Runcw i, was also awakened by the noise and he.disiinctly heard his wardrobe which stood about an inch off the wall rock against the wall. Many similar movements of furniture were heard. Later still a brilliant sash of lightning ac- companied by thunder came over the town. During .the morning, snow fell heavily and covered the streets vrith a white sheet. About noon it commenced to thaw and the roads were consequently in a wretch ed condition.

div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL ,SOCIETY.
div.p: THE RUNCORN MUSICAL ,SOCIETY.
"THE MESSIAH."

The Runcora Musical Society held a grand perform- ance on Thursday night in the Public Halt when Hamlet's " Messiah " was given. The principals introduced were all new to Runcorn audiences with the exception of Mr. Humphreys (tenor). The others were Miss BOA New- combe, soprano ; Miss Sarah Berry, contralto; and Mr. Arthur Barlow,hass. Miss Newcombe is a native of Rae- corn, and is well-known in Runcorn, Widnes, and War- rington, and many of the large tosses. Sin) has a rich , soprano voice,and her visit te her native town was wel- comed. It may be here mentioned that her father was one of the founders of rhe old Madrilfal Club which after- wards blossomed into the Runcorn Musical Society. Mr. Newcombe and family afterwards removed to Penketh, Warrington,wheie they have since iesided. In addition to the principals there was a band and chorus .which numbered 120,under the conductorship of Mr. Frank H. Crossley. This is the Society's nintis season, and the third time they have given" The Messiah." The chortle was well balanced,etrong in street:sand was particularly effective in their reuJering of "And the glory," "For unto us a child is hour" "And with stripes," "Lift up your heads," " Hallelujah," and "Worthy is the Lamb." Miss Newcombe acquitted her - self well throughout and her rendering "Rejoice greatly" and "I know that my Redeemer Booth," was of a finished character and was loudly applauded. Miss Sarah Berry was deservedly encored for her beautiful rendering of the solos, " He shall feed His • Sock," and "He was despised." "But Thou did'st not leave" and "Thou shalt break them," were rendered with good effect by Mr. Maldwyn Humphreys. Mr. Arthur Bar- lowgave a brilliant exposition of "Why do the nations," "But who may abide," and " The trumpet shall sound." At the interval the orchestra under the leadership of Mr. R. Pearson, of Warrington, played the "Dead March" (Saul) in memory of the late Mr. J. Brundrit, ‘J.P., president of the Society. Mr. A. S. Musgrove, A.R.C.0., was the organist. There was a fair audience.

div.head: HEAVY FAILURE OF LOCAL FARMERS.
div.p: HEAVY FAILURE OF LOCAL FARMERS.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Ceurt n Friday last week, before air. Registrar Ridgway George Percival and John Percival, of Parkside Farm, Preston Brook, farmers, trading there, and at 137, New- port-st., Bolton, Lancashire, as "G. and J. Percival," previously trading at 11.1, Newport-st., Bolton, and 29, Fold-street, Bolton, as hay, straw, and potato dealers, under the style of "The Cheshire Farmers' Supply Stores," and at the Market Hall, Bolton, and Greenway-road, Runcorn, as cream and milk dealers, appeared to undergo their first public examina- tion in bankruptcy. The gross lia.bilities were £12,184 183. 3d., expected to rank at £11,790 19s. 9d., and the assets after deducting all charges £1,979 4s. 2d., leaving a deficiency of £9,811 153. 7d.—The bankrupt, George Percival, had filed a statement of his separate affairs, disclosing one unsecured claim for £374, but no assets ; and the bankrupt, John Percival, a like statement, but disclosing neither liabilities nor assets. The causes of failure as alleged by bankrupts were want of capital; low prices of produce; •loss by fire in March. 1595; losses of farming dock through disease; dry summers diiring last two years; excessive rains during the last two months ; and bad debts in connection with the Bolton business. The unsecured liabilities, were :—£5.304 13s. yd. for money lent and bank overdrafts ; £3,273 2s. 7d. for goods and work done; £943 17s. 2d. for cattle and sheep ; £847 19s. for rent; £44, for grai:ng; £l2 153. 4d. for legal and accountancy charge.; £1,438 for balance of purchase money of farm. e and effects, and £l2B 123. ld. for - freight, sack hire, &c., &c. At the conclusion of the di2tribution Master Moulton presented a beautiful bouquet to Mrs. Wood. Master Timmins also thanked her tor distributing the'prizes. The Chairman said the prize distributi,m, which he was certain they had all followed with interest, especi- allylthose who had received prizes,was the primary object of the meeting that might. A complete system of prize- giving such as obtained in their schooli was a wonderful incentive to regular attendance and hard work, and it had without doubt played an important part in raiinge the schools to that high standard of efficiency which they had now attained. (Applause.) The prize fund ho said had been established eight years, and £7O had been raised and distributed to the scholars for successful work, diligence, punctuality, and regular attendance. A limelight lantern with slides to the value of £3O had also been provided in aadition to the one presented by- Sir J. T. Brunner M.P. The prize fund was estab- lished to prornOte habits of punctuality, '&c. By in creasing the average attendance on which graets were paid it had enabled the school to be carried on at a less expense to toe rates. The whole of this money had been raised by the efforts of the teachers themselves. —(applause)—assisted by Mr. livnnersley, H.M. In- spector of Schools, who delivered a lecture in the autumn, the proceeds of which were devoted to the prize fund. Whilst this distribution was the primary object of the meeting, it was also a meeting by which parents and ratepayers generally were brought into con- tact with the School Board and their school. He thought the people of Runcorn took a great interest in the Board Scheol,as evinced by the large audience present. Their schools had attained a high mark of efficiency and quite recently the Ins' ector ranked therm amongst the highest in his division. (Applause.) That high position had not been gained without hard work,and it could not be main- tained witheut still harder work. It would be abso- lutely necessary for them to work in the future as in the past. He felt sure the Board and the teachers would throw all their energy into the enterprise. Regular at- tendance was the foundation of success. He implored parents to send their children punctually and regularly to school, and to encourage them to take advantage of the educational facilities now within their reach. It was far better and a safer heritage than leaving them a large fortune. (Loud applause.) In conclusion he said they owed a deep obligation to the over-burdened ratepayer. The great bulk of the money was spent on education, but yet he felt certain that if anyone wilful go carefully through the local expenditure, be could feariosly assert that no item yielded such rnagnifiont results as educa- tion. The very best investment of this country was money spent on education. Mr. Pritchard, in proposing a vote of thanks, said they owed a great obligation to Mrs. Wood for her kind- ness in attending and se graciously distributing the prizes. (Applause.) Mr. Johnson seconded.
_ Rev. W. H. Stables, on behalf of Mrs. Wood, thanked them for the very kind reception given to her, and also for the kind words uttered by Mr. Pritchard and Mr. Johnson.
Mr. Moulton proposed votes of thanks to the donors, and to the Chairman.
Mr. G. Mess seconded and the propwition was carried.
TEE PERFORMANCE.

A member of children then took part in the comic operetta " Marjerie." The scene of the play is laid in a woodland glade near Baron Honeysweet's Castle. He bere entertains his guests and tenants at the coining of 2.e of his only son Sir Reginald. The Baron's archers,a bevy of pretty &racier girls, and a group of tradesmen offer their congratulations, and amuse the company by their sprees. Luncheon is new served, and during its progress there enters a poor girl (Marjorie), who has sun away from her suppesed father--a tramp—and the Baroness kindly takes her into her service, Just then the jester upsets a hive of bees,and the whole company, except the jester, retire in haste. Hearin e footsteps he reeceals himself, while a tramp enters and begins to steal the silver. Talking aloud he reveals the fact that he was opine a footman in the service of the Duchess of Flimertv-Funr, and being dismissed, he stele the Dowager's child. The jester tries to arrest him, but failive to do so, he informs the Baron of the affair, and the whele cempany search the woods, and are success- , i bringing the tramp before the Baron fcr punish- ment. Pe —nfesses his fault a d is pardened, while Marjerie is, e, great joy 4 'erre to her mother. The children displayed th respective parte in an admirable manner,and ke eeaudience in eood humour all the evening. eh eters Baron Honeyaweet, (Correia to the Deere ) Master A. Burton; Sir Reginald (The Baron's son e heir) Master T. Williamson, or Master H. Stanway ; the tramp (the Dowager's old foot- man) Master S. Lane ; the clown (the Baron's jester) Master James Benner ; the Baroness, Miss Nellie Tem- perley ; the Dowager (Marjetrie's mother)eliss Lillie Hill; majosie (A wandering outcast) Miss Sissie Curzon ; courtiers, peasants (male and female), school girls. archers, gipsy girls, tradespeople. ssrvants, (male and female.) etc. Scene—l. woodland glade, near Honey- sweet Castle. The children were trained be the head teachers, Mr. J. F. Mutton, and Miss A. M. Kilburn, who were aided by their assistants, Messrs. J. C. Cra.gg, W. R. Joynson, L. W. Jeacock ; Misses A. Acton, E. Watts, C. W. Holden, B. Hill, M. Simi:in, E. H. Hough. E. Ellison, A. Porkies. and E. McLean, to whom great credit is due for the efficient manner in which the children were trained. Thanks are also due to Mr. Ronald Jeaceck for the admirable way in which he did the " make-up" of the scholars. The scenery was kindly lent by Mr. W.. H. SIR 3. T. BRUNNER, M.P., AT RTTNCORN.
UNVEILING A MARBLE TABLET.

Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart., M.P., visited Runcorn on Thursday evening for the purpose of unveiling a marble tablet which be presented to the Runcorn Co-operative Society in commemoration of the first committee of the .Society and of the establishment of co-operation in the • district. Mr. W. E. Dadley presided and was supported by Sir John, Messrs. W. litlClo9, T. Riley, W. Rushton, J. Evans, J. B. Arthur (Irst setretary),J. Shaw (present secretary), W. Dwyer (vice chairman), Stubbs, Moores,l Hartles, dewyer and Lidston. The Chairman in opening the procesdiags said, in the name of the members of the Co-operative Society he heartily welcomed Sir John into that room on the occa- sion of the unveiling of the tablet which he bad so kindly presented to the members of the society. (Ap- plause.) They would agree with him in calling that a red letter day in the history of the local society. When t ley contrasted the times the tablet commemerated,the consption of the working classes with the present times I they would see that the workingmee were much better off now. In the early days the workingman Old not realise the sense of his responsibility. But then a spirit dawned on the workingman and the Rochdale PlJneers sprang up, and so he found out that he could take care of his own savings and someone else's too They knew that if co-operation was to go ahead they most educate their people. This was done and the society bad flour- ished. Since Sir John Brunner's last visit the Runcorn branch bad done something in the way of educating their members. Mr. W E. Gladstone said that he had the greatest hope of its country when public men Hie Sir John Brunner took an interest in co-eperation,and he (the Chairman) Sri:ought they ought to consider them- selves proud in having a visit,from Sir John under these •auspicioes circumstances. (Loud applause.) Sir ;ohn Brunner, M.P., on rising was loudly cheered, sesi it was now a good many months ago since he at- ',ended their annual meeting and had the pleasure of addressing them. He remembered very well speaking to them on the subject the Chairman had alluded to—the subject of education—and very much charmed was he to hear that shortly after that visit the committee of the Runcorn Co-operative Society had decided to introduce the system of lectures upon co-operation which he trusted would be the means of confirming their faith and adding largely to their numbers. At that time he heard a good Weal of the spirit of manfulness and self- sacrifice that animated the members of the first commit- tee. He was full of admiration of the work they had done, and he thought that something should he done to commemorate their worke in some prominent form. Be suggested to the committee that a memorial tablet should be erected in the beautiful hall, upon which should be inscribed the names of the first committee and secretary. He was present that night for the purpose of unveiling that tablet to their memory. It was with heart-felt pleasurs he came to draw the curtains aside and present it to them. It was a memorial of good work done. (Applause.) He was very happy to say that it was not k memorial of those gone trom them. Happily there were living no fewer than five naernbers of the first committee. The treasurer, be regretted to say, had gone, but he was proud to see his neighbour, Mr. Arthur, who was the first secretary. (Applause.) Pleased he was to say, that four of the first committee who were living resided in Runcorn, and were present that night. One of the committee was also liyine in London, The society could not ascertain his address, and so he was not present. Mr. Joseph Hughes was the gentleman'a name, and he was proud to say be is a Crimean veteran ; be was also glad to hear that his ser- vices in the Navy had been looked to by a grateful Government who had given him a pension. (Applause.) It was perfectly clear that those who paid his pension would undoubtedly know where he resided. If the com- mittee had written to him be would have found him by inquiring at the Admiralty. However, a letter of regret at his absence should be forwarded to Mr. Hughes. Sir Jahn then proceeded to the centre of the building and ne unveiled the tablet amid loud applause. The tablet is composed of marble and at the head is a sheaf of wheat, spade and a sickle, across which is a band bearing the words " Labour and Wait." Then follows the names ef the first committee, viz. :—W. Rhodes, J. Bailey, T. Riley, J. Clucas, W. Armstrong, J. Hughes, J. Evans, J. Howard, treasurer, and J. B. Arthur, secre- tary ; after which were the following words :—" To commemorate the first committee of this society elected in 1862 and the establishment of co-operation in Runcorn through their disinterested and self-sacrificing labour, this tablet was placed here en the suggestion and at the cost of Sir John T. Brunner, Bart., M.P., and was unveiled by him. 17th Deeeruber, UK"

Proceeding, Sir John said he was perfectly satisfied that there was no man or woman present that night but who would remember for many years to come the occa- sion of that evening. Might the unveiling of that stone be an incentive to equal if not greater labour, and to equal devotion to that which had been shown by good mm n whose names wore commemorated on that stone. Ile wished the Society prosperity and increasing useful- ness. (Loud applause.) The Chairman said he had great pleasure in handing Sir John one of the Co-Operative Society's annuals on behalf of those present. They had always found the an- nuals full of practical information, such information as would interest Sir John in kis official cspac,ty as repre- sentative of this division. He banded it to him as a very slight token and small memento of his kindness. The Chairman then handed the annual to Sir John arid loud cheers.

Sir John Brunner in accepting the "annual," said it was impossible to hear such words as their Chairman had just spoken without being touched. It was but little he did as compared with what he ought to do. Mr. J. E. Muorhouse (Oldham), direstor of the Co- operative Wholesale Society, said he felt it a degrecof pleasure to be present at this ceremony. Few men of high social position in the land took so much interest in the doings of the working-classes as their worthy repre- sentative had taken that night. Be thought that any gentleman taking an interest in this movement was de. ing an honour to himself and an honour to the general public. They looked upon Mir great co-operation move- ment as the lover of the elevation of the working-classes of this country. (Applause.) The members ef that Run- corn branch tad something like L'44,000 pounds in share and capital. Had it not been for the co-operative movement very little of that money would have been saved. Runcorn had been one of the most faithful societies connected with the great federation which had connected with it over 1.500 societies. This business amounted to ten million pounds and so far as this year was concerned the Co-operative WhelesaleSoeiety would have an increase of over one million sterling in business. (Applause.) They were now trying to better the agricul- tural depression, as far as butter was concerned they got supplies from Denmark, Sweden, Ireland and other countries. In days gone by Ireland was the greatest centre for butter trade and supplied the whole country. But it had got behind, and foreign competition came in. The Wholesale Society believed in bringing back the butter trade to Ireland. They had nine or ten creameries working in that country in order to teach the Irish farmers the quickest and most economical way. They were trying also to do this in England and he considereil this a move in the right direction. (Applause.) They were not only trying to become shopkeepers, but were also trying te become employers of labour. Mr. Arthur, secretary of first committee, said after having, heard such eloquent addressee that night be thought there remained nothing for him to say. In looking back over the past 30 years,—perhaps a little more—there was no doubt that they stood shoulder to shoulder and got co-operation from a small into a gigan- tic movement. They had heard from Sir John Brunner a very sympathetic address, and he was sure they would give him a hearty cheer. Mr. Rhodes seeended. Mr. Riley proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Moorhouse.

. . Mr. Evans, in seconding, gave a brief history cf the local branch. Me said, a number of them got togothei and decided to have a lecture. The lecturer, a Mr. Richardson, cave them a lecture on co-operation, after which he took several of their names. A committee was formed on July 12th, 1862, and a she..p was opened on July 26th in the came year. The &peak*: Was. a commit- tee man for about two years, aoditor fer three years, and was elected treasurer on the retirement of Mr. hovrard. 'the total amount of shares investe in the society at commencement was about £6. Mr. Moorbouss proposed a veto of thanks to the Chair- man f r presiding. The proposition was seconded and unanimously carried, and the meetin4 terminated.

His Honour Judge Wynne-Ffoulkes had a cue before him on Thursday mLrning at the Warring- ton County Court, in winch Messrs. Gough and Co.,furniture Gealers, Winwick st., Warrington,claime damages from Mr. Joseph Harrison, J.P., the high bailiff, for neglect of duty in connee,ion with the levying of an execution. Mr. _Miley, of St. Helens, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Arthur Browne represented the defendant. His Honour said he could not try the case as it affected an official of his Court. It must go either to St. Helens or Widnes. He had already informed the plaintiff's solicitor as to what he intended to do with the case.
Mr. Browne said they would object to go to St Helens—the home of Mr. Riley. His Honour: I have to decide which Court it shall be.
Mr. Riley said either Widnes.or St. Helens would do for hie client.
Mr. Browne said Mr. Riley had consented to ga to Wigan.
His Honour: Well, Wigan is not so far from here.
Mr. Browne: It is the same distance from War- rington as St. Helens. _
Mr. Riley said he quite concurred in the sugges- tion that the case should be tried at Wigan. His Honour: Thep I will transfer the case to Wigan.

div.head: PARR HALL SATURDAY CONCERT.
div.p: THE PARR HALL SATURDAY CONCERT.

In contrast with most of the concerts held in Parr Hall under the auspices of the Parr Hall Committee, there was Only a poor attendance on Saturday eveaing. The programme went off well, however, and the concert was productive of enjoyment to the majority of the aud- ience. There were eight artistes, as rollows :—Soprano, Miss Lottie Herod ; contralto, Miss Funny Sault ; tenor, Mr. etalter Lawley; basso,ldr. Dennham Barn; violinist, Mr. Tom Boothroyd, concertinist, Mr. T. Ry Fond; hum- orist, &c., Mr. Harry Collins; and piauiste, Miss Pauline Stewart. With such an array of vocal and instrumented talent, the programme was necessarily a long one,and in the main encores had to be denied the audience. The 'singers made a most efficient quartette party and their singing of" Regular Royal Queen," (Gqndoliers), " sob. bing," (Caldicott), "Gipsies Laughing Song," and "Good Evening," (Seymour Smith), furnished one of the meat enjoyable portions of the entertainment. "Sobbing "was perhaps the exception,aa it degenerated into a farce which would have be.ter suited a humorist than four serious singers. Miss Lottie flerod's clear soprano was displayed to advantage in " Esmeralda," and " The Spanish Gipsy," a type of song for which she has apparently a predilection, and certainly a capacity for rendering. Mr. Walter Lawley was the greatest success of the evening, and an encore for his Bag inter. pretation of 'Take a pair of sparkling eyes," WVI insisted upon, and he complied with "You'll remenstsr me." Again, in" Let me like a soldier tall," Mr. La w. ley's strong and melodious tenor voice called forth enthusiastic applause, and his encore song "Madeleine," was no less successful. Miss Fanny l,ault and Mr. Dana- ham Barn i both gave satisfaction with the ',sage. entrusted to them. Mr. Tom Evothroyd lost none of his reputation as a premising violinist by his execution of " Air Vatic " " Darcla), and " Salterelle " Another local performer was Mr. T. R. Ford, wanes quota to the performauce was t. couple of concertina soles, "Blue Bells of Scotlaud," aid " Melodie in F." Be played on two instrument's, large and small, extracting from heth some pretty music. Skill and taste were ovident in Mr. Fund's playing and hr fully merited the encore to his wvond piece. Mr. Barry Collins could hardly be styled a success as hum- xtrist, but he was a most novel and eecentf c per- former. Soles on banjos and other instrument; were accompanied by very tuneful whistiiug.and ROM.) of his ditties were amusing. "Pushing tht to clouds .Iway,” and a trick le..nje solo were about Mr. Colliat' best efforts. The eis a diversity in his accomplistments which found favour, though humour is cortain.y not his forte.

Correspondeats at a distance describe it as the most serious which trui oc- curred far many years, but beyond alarming a great many sleepers, who imagined that their house, ware collapsing over theist cr that hurgtars were attempting to break in, it doss not appear to have had maly toward effects, The en o exception to this statement the experience *f lllreferd, where a woman i to have died from fright and the pinnacles of the Cathedral and of Bt. Before the Mayor and ot' ,er magistrates at the War- rington Police Court on slenclay, Arthur Palkett and Thoma,,s Power, of no settle I abode, were charged with obtaining on Saturday 131 a forged order upon James Tayler, two boxea of con 7ectionery.—The Chief Con- stabla applied for a week s remand in order that he might comple the evident e and make some inquiries as to the antce,edents of thE prisoners. He said it was a story of a t %refaced swit die. At half-past eleven on Saturday tfght the prism ers were seen in Church-st. with two b oces containing sweets. They had been en deavourinr to dispose of 'hem for considerably under their cash value. Sergean Cheney and P.C. Chrimes questions I the men, and ola of them made a rambling staternect to the effect that he had obtained the sweets from a person named Slater at St. Helens. They were hrtught to the P )lice Station, and subsequent inquiries elicitor! the fact that at lalf-past eight the prisoner Palkett'went to James Nay or's shop, 21, Queen-at.,with a paper purporting to be an order from a Mrs. Taylor for various sweets. Mr. Ntylor had a customer of that name, and not being suspicious of the man he gave him the gonds. When the pris)ners were confronted with these facts in the police offi( e, they wavered, snd at last made statements to the effect that Power had written the " order " and gave it l:o the other man to present, their object being to ohtr.iq money to tide them over Sunda., ,and to provide tl,emaelves with some articles to hawk na Monday. They were strangers to Warrington, and hal come from LiverpooL—The magistrates re- manded the prisoners for seven days.

She got her father away,and thcn the prisoner struck her on the head and face with his fiat. and attempted to kick her. —Pris .ner's father corroborated, and stated that before he went to the dolr prisoner had broken a window of the house with a bucket.—Detective-Inspector Monag- han stated that prisoner hal been convicted thirty times previously. and was a good-for-nothing corner- man—He was sent to gaol for six months with hard labour.

It appeared from the evidence that the prisoner was ejected by a constable from the Ram's Head, Earlestown. and failed to appear to answer the summons. A. warrant was issued, but he was not arrested until the pre- vious night.—The magistrates fined him ss. and costs. A second charge was then preferred against the prisoner. th it of being drunk and disorderly on the 11th inst. at Haydock. He was also fined ss. and costs on this count. ASSAULT ON a PAINTER .A.T LBORNE —John Fearicks WAS summoned for assaulting Frederick Scholes, at Golborne on the 7th December. He pleaded not guilty. The complainant, who is a painter, residing at 15, Cross-street. Golborne,stated that on the date named he was walking up Legh-street in I company with a young lady when the defendant met him and said he was just the man he wanted. Witness told him that he hadn't time to speak to him, but the defendant fol- lowed him a short di stance, and then caught hold of him by the coat and pulled him to the fioor.The defendant struok him in the face, cutting hie lip, and also kicked him five or six times on the holy. Witness could not say who picked him up.—Ellen Ashton, 69, Legh-street. Golborne, said she was in company with the complainant on the date named. She saw the defeadant thump the complainant in the moutheand also kick him. The complainant was dragged by the defend- ant into the middle of the street —The defendant said the complainant had been speaking in a slanderous manner 'against him and his wife and he wanted the c implainant to disprove his statements. He denied that he kicked the complainant, stating that the complainant received his in- juries by falling on the cuebstone,—John Crabtree, 12, Livia- , street, Golborne, gave evidence for the defence.—The magis- trates fined the defendant ss. and costs. 13XTRSORDINARY ASSAULTS BY A GlRL.—OarOllne Hayes,a girl about 15 years of age. of Golborne, was charged with hav- ing on the 18th inst. at Golborne assaulted Gertrude Shirley and further charged with assaulting Elizabeth Jane Jones' at the same time and place. —The defendant was accompanied by her mother whi produced a doctor's certificate, The malls- trates, after reading it decided that the defendant should not be present during tiae hearing of the case.—Gertrude Shirley 14 years of aee, living with her parents at Stubshaw Cr. 'as, near St.lielensand who appeared ha court, with her face terri- bly disfigured.stateel that on the date named she was returning home from Golborne mill in company with Elizabeth Jones and another girl when she was met by the defendant in Gol- borne-road. Without speaking to her, the defendant struck her a violent blew on the face either with a poker or a piece of iron. It was dark at the time, and she cauld not distin- guish what it was She fell to the ground, and some time elapsed before she came to herself agein.Her face was covered with blood, as was also the face o the girl Jones. —ln cross- examination by the defendant's mother, she denied that she had ever called the defendant names, or struck her w‘th a can —Elizabeth Levies, 15 years of age, living at Stubshaw. Cross, said she was in company with the last witness on the night of the date named. She saw the defendant strike Gertrude Shirley on the face, with something she brought from under her apron. Shirley fell f,o the ground. and blood streamed down her face.—Mrs. John Shirley deposed that her daughter came home with her face bleeding from a wound over the eye. She at once took her to the doctor.--Bliz Jane Jones, 14 years of age, of Stub- sbaw Cross stated that she was also struck on the face by the defendant and Eliz Levies gave corroborative evidence. They had never spoken to the eetenciant.—Mrs. Hayes mother of the defendant, said her daughter had never committed an assault of that kind before. The only reason she could assign for it was that the girls at the Golborne mill had proveked the defendant. The doctor had been attending the defendant for over twelve motel hs for epileptic fits. She was seized with them about once a fortnight. Witness had not told the doetor of the present charge. He had told her the girl must not be excited. The Bench retired to consider their decision and on their return, the Chairman said it Was an exceedingly difficult and painful case. He advised the defendants' mother to see the doctor at once to tell him of what had occurred for they were of opinion that the girl was not responsib!is for her actions at times. The present case would be dismiss d on payment of costs on condition that Mrs. Hayes carried out the suggestion made. Blackburne stated that at 6 o'clock on the afternoon of the date named. from informa- tion he received he proceeded to Lodge-lane, Haydock, and there saw a bay pony lying on the side of the road detached from a cart. lt appeared to be in pain, and on examining it, he found an old sore about four inches by three inches superating very much. The matter was running down both sides of the pony's back. On the advice of witness, the de- fendant had the animal slaughtered. The pony was unable to get on its legs.—George Cawley stated that at noon on the date named he saw the pony in question in Church' street, Haydock, attached to a cart laden with furniture. He afterwards saw it in Lodge- lane lying at the side of the road. It was unab'e to get up. and a large wound was discharging matter—The &•fendant said the wound was skinnel over when he started out in the morning. He thought it must have been rubbed against when the pony fell down.—Heury Pickles. of Ince, spoke to the condition of the ormy when it started out.—The Chairman said the defendant was a perfect brute. and the magistrates did not know whether they should not send him to orison without the option of a tine. 13u1 as that was the first offence, he would be fined 40s. and costs.

Mrs. Austin, who lived in the same block, came out of a house near complainant's and said " I -will show you what I can do; you , have gone and reported me about my dog." She wrongfully sus- pected complainant of having given information. Without provocation defendant knocked complainant ,)ff the parapet and then followed her to her door where she scratched her face. Complainant came straight to his (Mr. Davies) office and he himself saw her f ice bleeding -Mrs Wrench corroborated.-Mrs. Ellen Warburton deposed to see- ing Mrs. Austin push complainant off the footpath, follow her and scratch her face, causing it to bleed--Rlizibeth Jack- son gave similar evidence.-Mr. Unsworth thought the case was a very paltry one Mrs. Wrench had the reputation of being mischievous in the neighbourhood. He alleged that Mrs. Wrench used bad languaze to Mrs. Austin and spat in the face of a Mrs. Monks. Defendant then called complain- ant a "dirty thing," and complainant struck Mrs. Austin the first blow with a string bag. They then struggled. He asked the bench to dismiss the case as complainant struck the first blow,-Mrs. Austin supported her soli itor's statement. Harriet Ann Monks and Rliza Jones gave additional evidence. RUGBY POO MALL. WARRINGTON v. WIGAN.

These clubs met for the first time this season at Wigan, on Saturday. Rain was falling heavily and the ground more resembled a morass than a football field. Barber was unable to appear for Warrington. The teams were : Warrington, full back, Heesom ; threequarters, Lawless, Cross, Moores, and Radford; half backs, Houghton and Higginbottom ; forwards. Taylor Dakin, Scholtze, Hill, Swift, Barratt, Roby, and Jolley. Wigan; J. Halliwell, full back ; Flowers, Jags, Walkden, and Dixon, three- quarters ; W. Halliwell and Dennett, half backs ; Brown Rigby, Benson, Blackburn, Walsh, Perkins, Catterall, and Collier, forwards. Warrington won the toss and elected to play with the wind. Brown kicked off and Radford returned to half way, where Flowers sent the ball in touch. A wild pass fell into Dixon's hands, with the result that he sprinted to the corner where he kicked in touch. This looked bad for Warrington but Houghton effected a fine relief to midfield. From the next scrimmage the ball was heeled strongly out and Lawless punted well into the Wigan half. A forward rush however saw the homes- ters again pressing and Warrington being penalised. Dixon made a fair attempt at goal. Then Wigan infringed the rules and Taylor landed the oval past the half way flag. Cross added another few yards and Dakin prevented J. Halliwell getting in his return. Loose dribbling almost gave Warrington a score and they secured a good positiflon under the home goal. Unfor- tunately Houghton was too eager and get his side penal- ised,and a good chance was wasted. Hill however re- turned the kick and Flowers was called upon to relieve. Warrington held the upper hand still and a round of passing between Houghton, Lawless, Cross, and Moores, and then back to Cross,ended in the latter kicking over the line. Radford rushed up and Scored a fair try. He was quite on aide but the referee,Mr. Priestly,of Brough- ton, would not allow the point. The visitors pressed strongly for some time but at last Dixon ran away and put Wigan well on the offensive again. Taylor had another penalty kick but it was charged lown,and Dakin broke away to the 25 line. Houghton kicked finely to the corner and Higginhottorn had an unsuccessful drop at goal. Half-time arrived with nothing scored. Bill restarted and after some desultory play Radford let the homesters in by kicking at the ball instead of falling upon it. Again it devolved upon Houghton to reliev3 which he did by a smart run and kick. Dixon was prominent with another good run but in trying to kick past Heesom he allowed the Warrington custodian to make a good mark. Another penalty kick fell to Dixon soon after but he could do nothing with it. Then Flowers had a turn and running quickly along touch he almost put the Wigan forwards over by kicking in front of them. Lawless saved in the nick of time. W. Barnwell passed out to Walkien who made a poor at- tempt at an easy drop. Up to time neither side could claim much advantage and play continued to be of the kick and rush character all tiarou'gh. Tne game con- cluded as a pointless draw.
LANCASHIRE JUNIOR LEAGUE

RUNCORN RECREATION.r. Sr. EIILUNS RECEIELTION A 'TRAIL—These teams played their return match in the above league, at Runcorn, on Saturday. Owing to the heavy rains during the past few days, the ground was rathet soft. As the Runcorn team were successful at St. Helens a few weeks back, great interest was taken in the game under notice by the home team. The visitors came with a fairly strong team, but the home side were without Sutton, who was assisting'Runcorn A team,and a couple of other players for whom substitutes had to be found. The St.flelens team played downhill during the first half, and soon made their presence felt in the home quarters, and in a few minutes from the start had scored a try, which was not converted. This early re- verse put the home team on their mettle, and they suc- ceeded in transferring play to the other end', but could make no impression on the visitors' line for a long time, although they kept up a prolonged attack. A chance came at lasi which was promptly taken, and a smart passing movement between Hopley and Hughes ended in the latter getting over near the corner flag, no goal being kicited. A couple of free ki3hs in close proximity to the home goal post availed nothing, and at half time the score stood at a try each. In the second half the visitors forced the game and gave their oppon- ents a lot of defensive work, but the home backs proved equal to the emergency and never gave them an open- ing. The game was contested in a very spirited manner, and neither aide had any advantage. When time was up, the match was left drawn. Final score t—Runcorn Recreation, one try,; St. Helens Recreation A team, one try.

RUNCORN ASSOCIATION V. BIIRTONWOOD.—These teams being drawn together in the above competition the tie was played off at Runcorn on Saturday. Neither team had taken part in the opening round -both having ap- peared in last year's semi-finals. The teams lined up about 2.40 and Winter having choice of ends decided to take advantage of the strong wind which was blowing from goal to goal. The following appeared to represent Runcorn :—Goal, Bough; full backs, Stoneley and Tim- perley ; half backs, Burrows, Jones aud Clarke; for- wards, Hulse, Burrow, E.'egan,Williams and Mitchison. Deegan started and Burrows tricxing Winter, endea- voured to mako headway but Sullivan relieved, F. Bur- rows ultimately sending out of play. From the throw in, the visitors left secured and made straight for goal but the home defence withstood the pressure for some time. Several corners were conceded by the Blues' cus- todian but all were successfully cleared Williams next essayed to make for the other goal but Winter once again put the ball in the home goal mouth and the ball was put through by the visitors centre but he being palpably off side, Mr, Mather did not hesitate to disallow the point. The home custodian mulling a difficult shot a little later, the visitors snapped the opportunity and number one was placed to their credit. This was sopa followed by a second, being a beautiful header from the visitors' inside right. Ur,!ed on by the spectators the blues made great efforts to reach the other end, and it looked as if they would certainly score, several shots being put in. Deegan,and Barrows made some pretty move- ments and were well backed by Jones, 'Burrows. and Clarke. The visitors, however, drove them back, Sullivan putting in some ponaeroas kicks, their outside left ultimately scor ed a good goal from a weak clear- ance by Timperley. Half time arrived with .he score 3 to nil in favour of Burtonwood. Jones obtained posses- sion on the restart and Font to Burrowa, who defeated his man and then transferred to Hulse, whose centre was allowed to pass across goal and over the line. The homesters played up in a most commendable manner and their efforts were at last rewarded. Jones shot in hard, and the custodian in saving placed the ball at Deegan's foot, who slipped it round the post in a twink- ling. The visitors put in some neat low passing after the centre kick, but met with a good defence. At length Williams received from Clarke (who had been distin- guishing himself in fine style) and sent across to the ex- treme right where Hulse obtained possession and piloted the sphere through at the corner with a neat shot. Elated with their success the blues played with great dash, but try as they would,' the homcsters could not draw level and had to retire from the field defeated by a single goal the score reading Burtonwood 3, Run- corn 2.

div.head: BURNING FATALITIES AT
div.p: BURNING FATALITIES AT
WA.RRINGION.

An inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Elizabeth Emma Leicester, a young woman. 22 years of age of weak intellect, was held in the Parade Room at the Police Station on Mon- day afternoon, conducted by Mr. S. Brighouse.— England Leicester, filecutter, 42, Tilley-street said he was father o! the deceased, who was 22, years of age. About 2.30 on Saturday afternoon he left his wife and daughter at home. On returning he was informed that his daughter had been burned. She was immediately conveyed to the Infirmary. She was subject to fits and was weak in her intellect. Elizabeth Leieester, mother of the deceased deposed that at ten minutes to eight on Saturday night she proceeded to the market leaving the deceased at home by herself. She asked a neighbour to occasionally look at the deceased in consequence of her being of Weak intellect and subject to fits. She had left her on Saturday in a similar manner on many occasions.—Mary Lee, next door neighbour to the last witness, stated that Mrs Leicester asked her to see the deceased at intervals during Mrs Leicester's absence. She had done so on previous occasions. Shortly after Mrs Leicester had gone witness perceived a smell of burning and went into the house where deceased was. She found the girl's clothing on fire, and she (witness) with the assistance of the neighbours extinguished the flames. The deceased' was then taken to the • Infirmary. Witness believed that the deceased had been attempting to reach a piece of pencil from the mantel-piece when her clothes became ignited.—tfurse Dobson said the deceased was ad- mitted into the Infirmary on Saturday night suffering from extensive burns all over the body. She died on Sunday morning about two o'clock She was unconscious the whole of the time.— Ver- dict. " Accidental Death!' Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest in the Parade Room on Wednesday afternoon, rela- tive to the death of Catherine Griffin, who was found dead, severely burned, early on Tuesday morning in the kitchen of her daughter's house.— Julia Moore said the deceased was her mother, and Ishe lived with her at 3, Chrimes'-yard, Bank-street. Deceased was 61 years of age. She slept in the kitchen of witness's house, and on Monday night witness went to bed at a quarter to ten leaving the deceased in bed in the kitchen. The bed was situ- ated about two or three yards from the fireplace. where was a rug between the fireplace and the bed About 12-15 the next morning, witness smelled somethiflg. burning, and went downstairs to the kitchen. Deceased was on the floor quite dead. The hearthrug was burnt, and the deceased's clothing had been burnt away Both sides of the bed were burnt.—ln cross-examination she admitted that the distance from the 'led to the fire Wag only about three feet. She found a cob of coal on the rug.— Inspector Cox deposed that at 1-30 a.m. on Tuesday morning he was called to the house of the last wit- ness. He found the deceased quite dead, and the clothing had been burnt about the body, rather more on the right side than the left. The bed on which the deceased had slept was in the kitchen and close to the fireplace. It Was evident that a good fire had been left burn- ing when the people went to bed, and that some of it must have fallen and rebounded on the sack near the bed. Right above where the fallen coal had bap burning, the mattress and bed clothing were burnt. Re believed the deceased had endeavoured to put the fire out herself as he found some of the clothing wet. There was no fireguard round the fire. The people in the house were quite sober.— The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death.'

-- CHURCH ROOM.—The second of the series of three lec- tures on "The Prayer Book and Sexvices of the Church in Ancient and Modern limes" was delivered by Mr. H. .j. Westbrook on Tuesday evening, the Rev. S. P. Gray presiding. The lecture • was copiously illustrated by slides shown through the lantern by Mr. H. N. Hough- ton. There was good attendance. The period covered was A D. 600 to 1549.

M. Vitiate. who led the charge of the Lancers of the Guard at Graveintte, and was left for dead on the battlefield with his skull cloven by a sabre cut, has just succumbed to disease at Granville. having surived his terrible injuries rather more than a quarter of a oentury. The Royal baron of beef, which is the principal dish on the Queen's sideboard on Christmae-day, is to be cut from a Devon ox which was fed on Her Majesty's Flemish farm in Windeor Great Park. The joint, having been roasted at Windsor Castle, is sent on Christmas-eve to Osborne, along with a boar's head and a woodcock pie, which are also placed next day on the sideboard in the dining-room of the Palace. The Queen receives a !ermine hure sanylier from the famous preserves at Syringe, in Hanover, as a present from the Emperor and another • comes from the Duke ef Coburg besides a quantiti 'of German Cakes and sweetmeats. The late Duke Ernest of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha was for many years in the habit of sending a case of Imperial Tnkay to Windsor as a Christmas present. This was the Prince Consort's favourite wine, of which he in- variably drank a bumper after dinner.

div.head: S iLFORD v. RUNCORN.
div.p: S iLFORD v. RUNCORN.

- - This engagement was decided on Saturday at New Barns, Salford. Rain fell heavily and the ground was in a sodden condition. W. Faulkner kicked off for Run- corn, and in short time Griffiths, with a good punt, took the play to the visitors quarter. A free kick to Salford was well followed up and Houghton prevented from re- turning the ball, which was kicked over the goal line, where it rolled into touch in goal. On dropping out from the 25-yards line the exchanges were fairly even until Woodhead and Llewellyn broke away, and led a dribble to the Runcorn quarter. A free kick fell to the visitors, but little advantage resulted from it, and Griffiths get- ting possession took a fine but unsuccessful drop at goal the ball going dead. Salford continued to have the best of the same, but Houghton was very safe at full back, and repeatedly relieved his side at critical moments very cleverly. At length a good passing run by Nixon, Butterworth, and Reece toek the ball to the home line, where Reece was brought down by Menwaring. Relief was soon afforded, and the ball rushed by the home for- wards out of danger. Give-and-take play followed, un- til Griffiths by quickly following up, prevented the visit- ing full back from getting in a return kick, and scrimmaging ensued in the Runcorn quarter. A free kick to Salford was taken by Griffiths, who dropped at goal, which be just missed, the ball going t hroueh the posts, but under instead of over the crossbar. Half-time was shortly afterwards called, neither side having gained a tangible point. Heath resumed the game after a brief interval, and Runcorn as once forced the pane. Free kicks were taken without advantageous result, but a fine passing rrin in the home quarter by Nixon, Reece, Myers and Warder mzt with success, Warder securing a try for Runcorc after pretty play. Houghton took the place kick, but failed to increase the value of the try. Shottly after this Crocker was compelled to retire injured from the field, and Salford finished the game with four- teen players. The visitors had then much the best of the play, and only once, when Pearson by quickly f 1- lowing up prevented Houghton returning the ball, were they likely to score. On the other hand, Runcorn found the home defence very strong, and also failed to again break through, the game ending in their favour by one try (three points) to nil. Teams :—Salford : W. Man waring (captain), full back; A. Pearson, J. Frame, W. Crocker and G. Fawcett, three-quarter backs; Ivoy Grey and B. Griffiths, half backs ; G. Heath, D. Fisher, W. H. Llewellyn, H. Davies, S. E. Hanson, J. Fields, G. Fisher and H. Woodhead, forwards. Runcorn : Houghton,full back; T. Warder, J. B itterworth, H. Myers and W. Reece, three-quarter backs; J. Faulkner and J. Nixon, half backs ; W. Faulkner (captain), J. Langley, H. Far- mer, R. Lightfoot, S. Johnson, A Taylor, J. Shepherd and F. Gayter, forwards, Referee, Mr. E. Turner, Wurington.

WARRINGTON "A" V. WIGAN "A. ".—Despite the un- favourable state of the weather the attendance at the Wilderspool enclosure on Saturday was an excellent one. Wigan made the journey minus two of their players and consequently had to take the field with only thirteen men. Playing against the wind the locals had consiier- ably the best of the opening half, and the smart com- bination of the forwards gave ample scope for the backs to show their skill. Inaccurate passing by Grace spoiled many favourable openings, and it 'was not until the 1 game was twenty minutes old that Cooper managed to I score after a fine run. This try was the forerunner to an incessant attack, and despite the gallant efforts of Timmoney to place his side in a better position. the Warringtonians would not be deni,-d the !attack, and the outcome of judicious kicking saw the Wigan custo- dian in difficulties, and Edleston scored a point which , Boscow failed to improve upon. Near the interval the Warrington hacks passed effectively. and O'Brien got in, the home side leading at half time by three tries. On turnin2 round the Wa.rringtonians had all the best of it, and Wigan rarely crossed the centre line. The scoring was opened by laher wood, who notched a try as the re- sult of a brillant run, a point which he improved upon. O'Brien followed suit, and again did Isherwoool convert, whilst the same player a moment later dropped a smart goal from amidst a host Of opponents. Coneerted play between O'Brien and C)oper resulted in the latter racing infrom half vi iy; and this was the final score of the afternoon, Warrington winning by four goals (one dropped) and three tries (28 points), to Wigan nil.

RUNCORN " "Y. SALFORD " A."—At Runcorn before a poor gate. The visitors started.and Antrobus returned in touch at centre. Poole, Pendlebtirst, and Williamson engaged in passing, and Brown sent into touch. Again Poole got pesseesion,and passing took place between the last-named and Williamson, Richardson, and Gayter, the latter scoring. Antrobus failed to improve that point. On resumntiop,Salford got in the home half,where a free kick did not gain them much ground. A similar award to Runcorn followed, and play settled in midfield. A smart bit of passing between the Salfotd threequatters transferred play to the guncorn line. Another free kick was given to Salford,and an attempt Was made at goal, but it proviei futile.. On resumption Salford pressed, Loing away with a:rush. Brown,hovrever, stopped their progress. Sutton put a neat kick into touch, gaining ground. Poole, Williamson, and Richardson again put id some good passing, after which the Salford three- quarters displayed a pretty movement, but a knock-on spoiled the chance. Brown next got posseasion,and ran out to midfield. The visitors were not to be denied,and just nefore half-time rushed the ball over the Runeorn line,and Vipend scored. The kick at goal was a failure. Half-time: Runcorn" A" one try; Salford " A," one try. Alter the interval both ends were visited in turn. Salford got into the Runcorn half, hut the home team gradually got back to the centre. The visitors again got away with a rush,and got over the Runcorn line, almost scoring, the ball going in touch in goal. The sodden state of the ground,combined with a drizzling rain,now made the game uninteresting to the finish. Final result: Runcortr" A," one try ; Salford "A," one try.

div.head: IN THE INTERESP OF HUMANITY
div.p: IN THE INTERESP OF HUMANITY

For years, indeed one might almost say centuries. epilepsy has occupied the earnest attention of medical men, but until recently. the treatment of this terrible malady on a sound, scientific basis, has never been ar- rived at. The large number of persons suffering from one or other form of epilepsy makes the matter one of general interest, arid no greater service can to rendered to suffer 'Ts than to bring to their notice a well authen- ticated and perfectly reliaAe means of combating its effects, and effecting a lasting cure. When first intro- duced in Belgium, Dr. Fauyau's now celebrated remedy had to run the gauntlet ot professional jealousy, and an action at law was brought against the proprietor, in the Correctional Court at Liege, for illegal practice of medi- cine,but this prosecution,obviously undertaken with the express purpose of stamping out the treatment by other than medical men, did more to spread its fame than all efforts of its discoverer. Upwards of fifty witnesses. from the President of the Tribunal of Commerce, down- wards ; gave evidence in favour of the efficacy of the remedy, and the legal right of the proprietor to prepare and dispose of it was formally recognised and confirmed, It is to-day also the standard treatment for ,epilepsy in France where it is applied by medical men, and in the hospitals for epileptice. Among the numberless letters of thanks in Dr. Fanvau's possession, are many emanat- ing from persons whose social position renders it unde- sirable for their names and addresses to be made public, but who, nevertheless, are willing to reply privately to enquiries that may be made as to the beneficial effects of the treatment. These names and adresses,together with a little Pamphlet on the subject will be forwarded on ap- plication to Dr. FANYAXT (90,Great Bussell-street,London , W.C.).

The Russian Duke Nicholas continues to review French cavalry regiments and to insoect cavalry barracks. His last two inspections were at Charenton and St. Germain. He is received wherever he goes by a general of division. a general of brigade, and their staff. They conduct him in a open carriage to the review ground, where men and horses are put through their paces. He professes to be an adnairer of French cavalry, which once upon a time was the best in the world. It declined after Turenne, who regarded infantry and artillery as every- thing. Benaparte used cavalry shiefly to follow up the work done by artillery.

BY DORA M. JONES
TIII.-AJACCIO AND MARSEILLES.

S.S. Midnight Sun. For charm, for romance, for a mingling of grandeur with exquisite pastoral ssveetnese, I do net knew what can surpass the shores of the bay about Araccio. The town itself is small, and conteins nothing ot particular interesf, except its various Napoleonic associations. On landing we went at once, of course,to the historic house in the Rue Charles. It is one of a row of dingy tall white houses, and looks into a garden with an arbour of vines surmounted by e stone eagle and a fountain in the middle. An ivy plant is trained up the wall close to tile street, and we learned from an inscrip- tion that it was brought there by one Mat- hieu Grossetti, in 1874, from the Chapelle de St. Marie, at Chislehurst. The homely, shabby, but ample rooms, swept and garnished and empty, have a sert of sepulchral atmosphere about them. The blinds are down, the chairs, made in the fashion of a hundred years ago. are drawn up against the wall in stiff rows. You can conceive the sober little bourgeois household, the strong-minded motheie Madame Mere,as Napoleon always called her, Madame LiSecs in the Cor- sican speech—a sort of Roman matron with her five sons about her—pondering doubtless, as mothers do, on the future of her second boy, the young Napoleon with the beautiful impassive face. We saw his lithe room, ' which he occupied on the last time on his return from I the Egyptian expedition,—such a room as any young commis voyageur might occupy. Beyond the large salon with windows on either side, parquet flooring and a hideous pale wall paper striped with blue and red, they show you an adjoining room with a small trap door. through which it is said Napoleon escaped wh n the house was attacked by the partisans of General Paoli. A considerable portion of the beilding was burnt down but it has been restored with great exactitude, and cer- tainly gives an excellent idea of the milieu in whiele the future Emperor spent the most formative years of his life. We strolled through the principal square of the place, one side of which is open to the see. Here there is a statue of Napoleon on horseback— "Like a young god, with calm uneager face." We sat under the olives by the sea till it began to grow dusk, imagining how-delightfully one could spend three weeks in this enchanting island, which is cer- tainly in many-ways the ideal place for a walking vaca- tion tour. At last we reluctantly set our faces to the town. Stout peasant women passed us with free,swing- ing tread, carrying enormous baskets of fruit and vege- tables on their heads. Apparently they had walked down from thesmountain farms of the interior. Many of the women were aressed in black, with black hand- kerchiefs tied round tueir heads. All the next day we were coasting the Riviera, and those fortunete ones to whom a strong head-wind is a matter of indifference were admiring the Corniche, and painting out to one another— What Roman streng h Turbia showed In ruin on the mountain road. How like a gem beneath the city Of little Monaco, basking, glowed. ' We stopped at Villatranca, a sunburnt little place, climbing up a scarred hill to drop passengers; so that it was rather a maim' d company who sat down to dinner that evening, when Mr. Ju.tice Ross expressed with all his wonted geniality and grace the thanks of the party to Mr. Perowne and Mr. Lunn for shepherding them on their adventurous course. Of course, our excellent cer- tain and his officers were included in the vote of thanks that followed, and Mr. Perowne in his reply took occa- sion to say a word for the long-suffering stewards. We all felt rather melancholy that evening, as we an- ticipated the break-up of our happy fellowship of three weeks' standing, which on board ship is equivalent to a twelvemonth anywhere else, but on the following morn- ing we had no time to indulge in sentiment. We had to collect eur various impedimenta, to wait in the Custom House and sigh for a Zollverein which should dispense us from the tedious formality of examining luggage,and those of us who were going back to England bad to ar- range for starting either by the afternoon or evening train. Most of them chose the latter, so that many par ties were made up for seeing the town in the course of the day. High above the city, on a precipitous rock,stancls the old cathedral of Marseilles, Notre Dame de la Garde, a noble Romanesque building, with a guilt figure of the Virgin at the top,her arm extended in protection over the city. There is a hydraulic lift for the convenience of people who like that mode of transit, but there is really no occasion to spend sixteen SOUS on it. as the ascent by a winding road is perfectly easy. When you reach the platform on which the church is built, one of •the most magnificent panoramas imaginable stretches out before you,the city with Rue Cannebiere running up from the basin of the Vieux Port,tho magnificent quays,the dome of the new Cathedral near the Joliette Jetty, churches, and tree-planted boulevards and squares, all spread out like a map beneath you, and then,in the other direction, the wooded hills sloping to the sea,and beyond,the purple masses of the Corniche mountains, whilst at your feet you see the islande of the Bouches de Rhone. That for- tress on the smallest of the islands is the famous Chateau d'lf, from which, as "every scboolboy knows," Monte Christ° made his marvelloas escape. The wind was raging round the church and threaten- ing to blow us into the Mediterranean, so that we were glad to get inside. Here we were reminded of Ovid's reference to the votive offerings hung in the temples for the seaman's safe return. ehe walls were covered with small plaques,bearing the inscription, 'Reconnaissance is Marie " and a date. Evidently this is the sailors' shrine, high on its cliff,and buffeted by all the winds of heaven; and one could imagine how the eyes ef many a poor fellow have strained through the drifting spray for the gleaming figure of the Virgin on her watch-tower, and how heartfelt the invocation, Ave Maria, stella mans! The town was full of soldiers, Zouaves especially, and other African troops,in the picturesque blue and red uni- form, for a great demonstration was in progress. The bodies of six officers slain in January,lB94,,at Tacoubao, near Timbuctoo, had been exhumed, and were to be in- terred with all possible civil and military pomp in the Marseilles cemetery. I could not help being 'truck, while we waited, with the wiry look of the African troops. They were far from having the trim and neatly finished look of that highly expensive product, the British soldier ; they were shorter, slighter, not such fine men in short, ae our, but they looked as if they were inured to hard faring and accustomed to rely on themselves. They seemed full of keenness, readiness, and resource, and I could fully understand the natioe's pride in them, of which this day's ceremonial gave so striking a proof. An occasion like this helps one to understand what the word patrie signifies for Frenchmen—that romantic de- votion, which is like the enthusiasm of a lover. The time has gone by when it was the fashion to decry the qualities and sneer at the achievements of our great mad brilliant neighbour. May we not hope that the time may come Rome day, though just now it seems far off, when Frenchmen will realise that there is mere in English character and policy than can be summed up in the conveniept formula of" greed and hypocrisy." The time seems far off, but every agency which tends to bring men of different races and climes into amicable contact must shorten it. It may seem making too much of our little holiday to claim for it, and others like it, an international influence ; still we trust that we at least in future will bring to the consideration of our relations with other lands an idea or two the more, and a pre- judice or two the leas, from our cruise in the Western Mediterranean.
THE DUTY OF MR PRESS TO DISCUSS MATTERS OF PUBLIC INTEREST.

It is the duty of every individual, and especially the press, to distribute news and facts which tend to pro- mote general welfare, as by this means only will it reach all classes. Nothing is more deserving of publicity than the proper means or remedies which will ensure public health and prevent the ravages of prevalent chronic diseases, from which thousands lead a life of suffering and pain, hecause the proper moans and remedies are not known. Prominent among the remedies thus deserv- ing ef mention is Warner's Safe Cure. l'he universal verdict of thousands in Great Britain and Ireland, who have used it, leaves nc doubt as to its value, and we. have repeatedly reported facts regarding this remedy, and again bring before our readers a marvellous 'cure effected in the case of the son of Mrs Eliza Errington, 58, Silk Street, Ma.nnington, Bradford. Yorks., as illustrated by her letter of September 16,h before us, which reads : " Eighteen months ago my sots was taken seriously ill. The doctor, who attended him told pae that be had an abscess on the bladder, but after four months' treatment I was not satisfied and consulted six otter doctors. None of them told me what was the matter with hills, although he had been in bed over five months. As I was getting uneasy about him I told the doctors not to come any more, as I got a rec,mmendation as out- patient for the infirmary. One of the hospital doctors attended him at home six weeks, and then he told me it was a case of inside, and he was taken to the infirm- ary where he remained twelve Weeks, after which time I took him home. The doctors said there was n: cure for him, as he was suffering from Brieht's disease of the kidneys. Then I sent for Warner's Safe Cure,and thank God that he ever took it, or he would have been dead and buried long ago. But he is now well and walking about, and able to tollow his occupation. • This wonderful result is solely attributable to Warner's Safe Cure, and from all evidence we have gathered no doubt remains, but that in kidney and liver diseases and their developments this valuable remedy is the only reliable one to effect a speedy and permanent cure.
