EtTrIE AILURE OF WARRINGTON BUILDERS. efere Mr. Registrar Ridgway at Warrington, on Fri- _rs,eThomas Cross and Walter Cross, recently trading r the style of T. and W. Cross, at Longford-street, 41' ntfildtrs, cams up for a further examination in bank- • Y. the The baukrupts' affairs showed liabilities £1,897, assets, after deducting preferential debts £lo6,iea,v- -„II! deficiency of £1,791.11r. A. Browne again ap- ed for the creditors,and Mr.Forahavr represented the gebtors. Thom. as Cross, questioned by Mr. Browne, said he did " gnow why a number of leases had been taken out, Cr in his name, and some in the name of Walter ° Bs.—What object had you in view P—No object as I of.—Can you give any explanation of it ?—No „ Supposed you leased land in your name, and you Vrted building where did the money some from for 41;,1!118?—Islon't know.—Didn't it come from joint monies 4" You and your nephew raised from time to time on °rtgages ?—I suppose so.—Whe looked after the selling • i!(_1 buying P—My nephew.—Hew much did each of you out of the concern for wages P—Nothing.—Do you Zesti to say that you depended on what you received rtn the forge 2—Yee.—At whose request did you trans- o the lease at Hindley from yourself to your son ?—I know about the lease.—Didn't you take it from t France, Wigan ?—Yes, in the first place.—Your son 1:)0k :t over when there were £99 worth of bricks on the taf4„cl ?--Yes sir.—We have ample evidence that carts 'er carts filled with at if went from Warrington to put ,!sto these houses • who ordered the removal P—There -nothing of the kind removed wifli my kouvoledge. -I`l, it not a fact that you took stuff to Earlestown ?—I 1:11.t know.—What furniture have you removed P—l no things to take away.—Did you give your life IC to your son ?—Yes.—What did he pay you for i, ? toe Paid some doctors' bills.—Have you given Mr. Tiicrn- / a mortpge in your owniname a few months ago ? Cave never seen him —I suppose w atever Walter "s has arranged you have fallen in with it ?—Yes. Ir. Walter Cross was subjected to a tong cross-exam- tion by Mr. Browne. Asked whether he could ex- rain why gme leases were in his name and only a few nephew's name, the debtor replied that in some i,!es they took a large lease,and afterwards sub-divided- Oa order to raise enough money on it--You remem- Zr stating that only two loads of stuff went to Hindley; net did it consist of P—l cannot tell.—Whoordered its l'etnovai P—We did.—.-Where did John Cross get his 111°ney from to pay for the lease ?-11e worked for it. was the money paid F—ln cash.—You took a lease ilrs'and at Earlestown when you knew yen had land and piushs uninished in Warrington, didn't you ?—lt ,48 no use going on in Warrington.—No, be- youCr, had over-stocked the town with jerry ;uses ; who paid the wages ?-1 did.—Will you be sur- 11sed" to hear that you have paid in wages £5,329 in :tee years according to the bank book ?—Some of it Cut to pay eccounts.—How many mortgages have you ,ct during the past three years ?—I could not tell from elhory —Have you had thirty P—l could not tell.—By the • Registrar: You must remember it is your Uty to give all the assistance you Can.— ; Y Mr. Browne: Did you send to Earlestown a• mortis- niachine ?—Yes,—What became of it P—l sold it to a tan for 50i.—How much did you give for it ?—£B. ;Idn't you have a bicycle, and your wife as well P—No I cannot ride one.—Are there not several creditors kiln whom you have got goods since you filed your Detition sir.—You have given some creditors tb,ird and fourth mortgages P—l was compelled to do so ) get money.—Why did you show preference to som "trns P—Because they were pressing us.—ln whioh way _ L'llaey were threatening us with a writ.—Only threaten zy you ?---They had a writ ready.—You only got £2OO Zni 110 houses sold to the Warrington Investment Com- P—Tley were mortgaged in the Starr Bowkett l,..ety.—You sold Mr. J. P. Jones twenty-four houses ? es sir.--How much did he give you for them ?—He ,s64,Bme £,120 for 24 houses.—Who was the mortgagee in s case P—Mr. Thornton for one block, and Mr. Dobson m&I another.—When had you to sell them 2—ln August. Where is your furniture ?—I have none.—Whose was lue furniture then ?—Part belonged to my mother-in- and part my wife.—ls it not a fact that your wife °llg.ht the furniture with you money ?—No.—Did you 'Ct, an advance on the Longford-st. property ?—lt 'nngs tu my wife. Mr. Browne said he did not intend to ask any further restions that day but he was instructed to ask the „ebtors for certain accounts.—The Registrar suggested ,eat it w mid be better for the trustee to see the debtors • Otivately, and get all information he could. The Assistant Official Receiver said he would like to bar,ention that the:debtors when at the Official Receiver's ";_fnee were examined on all points with a view to 81ortenirg the examination. Their answers were very 2ften " I cannot exactly tell," "I am not sure,"" I uoa't knew." It was absolutely impossible to obtain any ,aeeurrat information. He thought the creditors were instified in asking for particulars with reference to the l'arious properties,and what had become of them. The Registrar told the debtors to furnish thetrustee • the entate with all particulars of leases and :the as- ll:gnu:tents thereof, together with ant' other information t e might require. If they did not give any information 'IIOY would run very great risks. Toeuxemination was be adjournedko January. Bth,

div.head: WARRINGTON TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION
div.p: WARRINGTON TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION
CONCERT.

tt, the commendable object of raising funds for th Te when' Orphanage and Benevolent funds, the Warrington and District Teachers Association arranged a concert which took place in the Parr hail cm Thursday evening last. The Warrington Teachers' Association, which is a branch of the Nat ior al Union of Teachers, has as its president,Mr. A. Wilcox, of the National school. Mr. J Wright, of the Board School, Daresbury, is 'vice-president; jr. G Brown, treasurer; Mr. T. Belden, secretary, and Mr. T. G-ordon, correspondent and secretary to the Benevolent and Orphanage fund. The bulk of the w,)rk in arranging the concert fell upon the latter gentleman, and he is to be congratulated on the satisfactory arrangements made. The attend- -4,11ce, considering the great number of concerts held recently and other attractions, was extremely Rood. The only alteration in the list of artistes announced to it4lte Part was the substitution of Miss Skeet for Madame u `golgans, who was nnable to be present through indis- Position. The other vocalists were Miss A. Richardson e•olattalto), and Mr. J. G. Howson (bass). Miss Skeet 18 not unknown to a Warrington audience, and has pre- Aliously sung at the Parr Hall this season. Gifted with a bright, clear, soprano voice she sang with considerable taste and effectiveness the songs which had been put down on the programme for interpretation by Madame korgans. Her three songs were "Flight of Ages," The Carnival," and "A Dream of Paradise," in which She gave evidence of her capacity to interpret songs differieg in sentiment and treatment. She was heartily applauded, but did not comply with an encore. Idles Richardson is the possessor of a charm- lug contralto voice and sings well. She made 4 good impression on the audience with her fringing of " When a little while has flown," that she was still more successful in her interpretation of "TwickenhamFerry."Her vocalisation was characterised by clear enunciation, and admirable expression ; she making the most of the piquant points in the story. Complying with the demands for an encore, she sang itvitli vivacity "Coming thrn' the Rye." Her conclud- -23,e song was "The Zuyder Zee" which further pleased sne F.udience. Mr. S. G. Howson was the only male 'vocalist. He opened with the rollicking song "Father O'Flynn,” in which he was fairly successful. In essaying the descriptive song" The Desert," Mr. Hewsou was not BO happy in his choice, although in this the pianist is able to introduce some fine touches which give tone and bieturesqueness. "The Night Watches" (Pinsuti) was Mr. flewson's concluding item, given with a great depth of feeling. Mention should also be made of the con- certed music with which the first and second parts of ,_sthe programme were opened. The f " irst was a trio Tlae '-/tieen of the Night" in which the three vocalists already tnentioned took part, and Miss Skeet and Mr. Harrison oPened the second part with a duet" The Siren and the Friar." Both were given in a manner that elicited applause. Miss Pelly Morgans Was the accompanist to the voe4iists. The instrumental music was provided by Warrington artistes. Mrs. W. B. Roberts ability as a piano and violin soloist is well-known by the Warrington music c`ving public. Her rendering of a rpmance by Thalberg dan air with variations on the piano •as very fine In her violin soloe,Mrs. Roberts has not been able to dis- Pease with her music sheets,as in the case with her piano liolos,which is perhaps a slight disadvantage, but, never- theless her execution of "Simple Aveu " (Thorne) and ' Sl,zerka " (Carl Bohm) was alike neat and tasteful. iier efforts called forth the continued applause of the audience, and she was constvained to bow her acknow- ledgments. Mrs. Roberts was efficiently accompanied on tha e piano in her violin solos by Mrs. Adams, wife of Dr. 4daine. One of the most interesting features of the con- cert was the performance of an orchestral band corn- -12,)5e4 of Warrington ladies, and conducted by Mr. A. idutto i. The pieces contributed were "Loin du Bal '- (Geter.), and " Intermezze " (Macbeth), in which Miss 4da Birtles performed a cello solo. The performance Ivas highly creditable to the bistro mentalists,anci the ap- Manse which greeted the termination of it was evidence "thlpnreciation of the audience. The humour of the evening was supplied by Mr. Wilson Blackledge—himself a member of the National Union of Teachers—and as his sabilities as an entertainer are so well-known in the town IS needless to say more than that he fully maintained ‘tle r,,putation he has gained.

div.head: EA.RLESTOWN &ND NEWTON.
div.p: EA.RLESTOWN &ND NEWTON.

*** CHRLSTMAS DAY.—As Christmas Day falls upon Friday next weak the " Examiner " will be published on Thursday. THE EARTHQUAKE SHOCK. The vibration of the earth which appears to have been generally felt over England,on Thursday morn- ing.made its presenne felt in Earlestown and New- ton. A large number of people seem !lo have felt 1 its effects,statements being made of disturbances in bedrooms chiefly, but there was really no state of alarm, as appetite to have been the case in some places. THE ENGINEERS' STRIKE AT EARLESTOWN. There is nothing new to chronicle in connection with the strike, which is dragging its weary length along, having now completed its second week. It is understood that pickets have been stationed at the works, but besides the half dozen who went in at Vicars' lass week, there have been no other seces- sions. There is a rumour that the Strike Committee purpose bring out the apprentices over 18 years of age, who are members of the society, but it is not thought that any action will be taken either one way or the other until after the Christmas holi- days. SHOCKING DEATH OT A FARMER AT

BURTONWOOD. On Sunday evening Mr. Edward Gleave, of Bur tvweed, met with an accident which 'resulted fatally on. Wednesday morning. It appears he has ibeeniin ill-health for some time, and on Sunday he in bed until late in the day, when he got up and Riming into the kitchen took hold of a teapot in order to get a drink. When in the act of drinking fronrthe spout he overbalanced himself, and falling backward4hiB head came in contact with the floor, causing severe concussion of the brain. Dr. Valen- tine wits sent for and he attended him, but the man died in great agony on Wednesday. The facts have been.reported to the Coroner. ". ACCIDENT AT THE VIADUCT WORKS.

On Monday. morning a young fellow named Joseph .:Marsh, employed as a labourer at the Via- duct W.Orks, when removing a cloth frame from the paipt shop to the crane on a bogey, by some means itamblecl, and, the frame falling across his chest, pinned him against some wheels. It was feared he was :very badly injured, but after being removrd.lome and medically atteuded,it was found that. hislinjuries were comparatively slight, but sufficient to keep him from work for several day.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARS
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARS

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Heil on Monday evening. Bro. W. Wilson, C.T., presided over a fair attendance of members. Arrangements were made for the New Year'e. fes- tival. A vote of sympathy and condolence was passed with Mr. awl Mrs. Cronin, in their sad ba- reavement, caused by the death of their son, Bro. W. H. Cronin. The question of a lantern enter- tainment was referred to the next session for con- sideration. The programme was carried through by the messbers of the St. Helens Great Heart lodge, Bro. A. Francis, presiding. Songs, glees, recitations, &c. were given. EARLESTOWN W ESLEYAN CHURCH. _ .

. _ On Sunday afterno-m, in aid of the Wesleyan day school, a musical Bervice, with selections from Handel's "Messiah," was given by the church choir before a large audience. Mr. W. Clare con- ducted and Miss E. LlGreenall presided at the organ. The items subrottted were, solo," Comfort ye," Mr. F. P. Clare; cAorus, "And the Glory " ; solo and chorus, "0 thou that tallest," Miss Holli- day and choir; solo' "Rejoice greatly," Miss May Clare ;organ solo, "Pa•toral Symphony " ; chorus, "Behold the Lamb of God " ; solo. div.p: MAKEBFIBLD_ HAILUIERE3

On Saturday the Makerfield Harriers opposed the Highfleld club at Newton in the second match of the season. The previous contest at Newton re- sulted in a victory fcr the Newton men by 6 points. This defeat stimulated the Highfielders to greater exertions, and a strong effort was made to whip up their very beet runnbrs. But the inelement weather experienced lately interfered with their good inten- tions, and they had to take the &Ids minus some one or two of their talent,vrith tile result that they fared worse than before. Whilst making every allowance for their non-success we must not over- look the very fine running of the winners. The hares led the peek a dance of about six miles through Winwick, laying a good trail "en route: Waywell, Williamson, and the veteran Smethurst made all the running, and drawing away from the "rack," finished in the order named, Forehaw and Shuffiebotham struggling gamely into fourth and fifth positions respectively-, for Maker- field, who got home once more, this time by 14 points. Sinking all antagonism loth sides sat down to a substantial tea provided by Host Chapman of the White Lion, and the rate at which the good 'things disappeared spoke eloquently for the appetising and healty sport, At the smoking concert which befittingly concluded the afternoon's enjoyment,mirth and music reigned supreme. Mr. W. Shaw alias Billy Richardson, and Mr. W. Kent, the embryo tragedian, pleasing the company im- mensely. Songs were sung by Messrs. Rylance,Wat- kinson, Williamson, Lewis,:and other iwell-knewn artistes ; aid Mr. M. P. ;Townsend and Sacretary Williamson debated in a masterly fashion. Mr. IW. Waywall proved himself as efficient at the piano as he is useful across country and helped to pass a most enjoyable evening. The Cross-lane harriers who assisted the above had a social evening in the Con- gregational Schoolroom the same evening. FATALITY AT THE TIADUCT WORKS. On Saturday morning, a sad accident, which ter- minated fatally, happened to a young man named William Henry Cronin, 19 years of age, a painter, employed at the Viaduct Works, Earlestown. About 6.45 on the morning, Cronin with seven others was engaged lowering from against a wagon, a cloth frame, which is similar to the top of a lurry, and is about 13 feet long by 6 or 7 feet wide, weighing 7 or 8 cwts.,with the intention of putting it on top of two others en a trestle. They had painted the underside of this frame, and when they had got it low enough for the trestle it suddenly slipped and the lower side shooting out came against another frame reared agaiast the wagon, causing it to fall forward, and before Cronin could get out of the way,it struck him violently on the head, fracturing his skull badly. Ile was perfectly unconscious,and was removed home on the ambulance stretcher. where he died two hours afterwards.—The inquest was held at the Viaduct Hotel on Monday morning by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner. Mr. Bland from the solicitor's office,Lime-street,represented the railway company, aid Mr. C. W. Emmett, assistant superin- tendent of the works, was also present. Evidence ef identification having been given by the deceased's father, and Mr. E. C. Martin, a verdict of "Acci- dental death" was returned.---The funeral took place on Tuesday, and was attended by about 80 of deceased's fellow workmen, about 20 of his Sunday school friends and several members of the football club with which he was connected. div.head: SOCIETY.
div.p: SOCIETY.

The third annual concert under the auspices of the above society was given in the Town Hall,New- ton, on Wednesday evening. The society, which is fairly strong numerically, has made much improve- ment under the leadership of Mr. P. H. Crossloy,and on Wednesday night they gave Remberg's cantata, "The Lay of the Bell." Fer some reason or other, there was only a poor audience, and it is feared the society may suffer financially. The leading parts in the cantata were taken by Mre.B.Clark(seprano), Miss 'Urquhart (contralto), Mr. G W. Kidd (tenor), and Mr. W. Collingwood (bass). It is needless to go into a description of the various numbers, as the cantata is so well-known. It will be sufficient to say, that Mr.. Clarke, Mr. Kidd, and Miss Urquhart discharged the duties devolved upon them, in an excellent manner. The major portion of the work fell upon Mr. Collingwood, who got through his task fairly well. The orchestra which was assisted by Mr. R 11. Pearson, of Warrington, WB4 much more successful than on previous occasions, and the accompaniments were well played. Mr. F. H: Crossley conducted throughout with ability, and Mr. A. E. Wykes accompanied on the piano. The second part of the programme consisted of mis- cellaneous items, which appeared to receive much more appreciation than the ,cantata. The feature ef this part was a pianoforte solo " Rhapsodie flougioise;" by Mrs- Leaster Dixon, whose execu- tion was of a masterly description. The other items were, characteristic piece, " Mandolieettc," orches- tra;. song," Thy Sentinel and I," Mr. J. div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, DECEMBER lB, 1896.
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, DECEMBER lB, 1896.
CHILDREN'S ENTERTAINMENT AND OPERETTA AT F. A. ttLESTO WN.

The officials of the Wesleyan Day School over a month ago commenced the arduous task of licking into shape, the material at their disposal for the presentation be- fore a critical public, of an operetta entitled "Merry Christmas." We cannot but admit that the task of pre- paring for such an entertainment as that which they put on the platferna of the Town Ball on Monday night, is a gigantic one, and sufficient to deter anyone whose heart and soul is not in the work fie= entering upon it. Mr. Burgess, however, with Mr. Braeley,Mr. Proucflove, Mr. Sandiford, and the other assistant teachers boldly undertook the duty, and the result both as to the suc- cess of the representation, and the attendance and ap- preciation of the public, must hav3 been eminently grati- fying to them. Whilst dealing with the, operetta, we must not forget the entertainment given by the infants, which preceded the oper- etta and for the success of which, Miss Williams the head mistress was responsible. Of the two, and taking into consideration the ages of the children to be dealt with, Miss Wdliams' task was perhaps the most trying, and doubtless she was considerably relieve(' when the public representation was at an end, and the plaudits of the audience were completed. As a preli- minary to the actual public appearance there was a full dress rehearsal at which several hundred of children were present, who frequently evinced their keen enj,y- ment by their spontaneous outbursts of appreciation. On Monday night the Town Hall was crowded in every part, in fact many were unable to obtain admittance, consequently the management have thought it desirable to repeat the entertainment. The first part of a long pro- gramme was devoted entirely to the infants under the care and guidance of Miss Williams. Their performance consisted of kindergarten games, drills, songs, and recitations, and as a whole, their per- formane was very well carried out,reflecting creditably upon their tutors, and Miss Eckersley who acted as prompter. Appropriately the programme was opened by a speech in parts, given by Lillie Wakefield, Nellie Lowe,Lottie Evett,and Mabel Allit,on. Following quickly on this was a kindergarten game, " The Flowers," in which the fairy,Florrie Potter,announced that she could summon any flower she pleased by the wave of her wand,which sh• fulfilled,the flowers such as tulip, daisy, forget-me-not, &c., were represented by Mary Edgar, Ada Sharrock, Ellen Wainwright, Jessie Allison, Martha Wells, and Olive Longwortb. The recitation "Jack in the Box" was naturally given by Robert Wilkinson who illustrated it by springing from a bex and announcing who he was. The • song "Eight little mothers" was prettily given br Annie Farrae,her, Mabel Hatton, Sissie Warburton. Minnie Jones, Pollie Green and Elsie Norris, each of whop carried a doll. The recitation " The foolish chicken" was naively given by Lillie Wakefield, as also was that given by Jessie Allison "Going to Market." The kindergarten game, "Births In the Beech Grave," was nicely carried out, the birds being Lottie Evett, and Annie Farmgher. The song "Little brown sparrow," was capitally sung, the sparrow being Edwin Davies. The concluding item was a musical drill with hoops, fans and wands by 24 infants, and under all the circumstances was well carr:ed out. _

The second part was devoted entirely to the operetta "Merry Christmas," and although it was not stated distinctly that it was a children's performance, still,see- iag that the major portion of the characters were under- taken by children,it would have been well if it had been left entirely to the children, with the exception perhaps of Santa Claus. We have,hosgeveroeo fault to find with the adults who took pert, and rendered valuable assist- ance, as they all acquitted themselves creditably. The first scene opened with the children all gathered toge-. ther waiting for Santa Claus, the chorus" Happy meet- ing " being a charming opening. This was fol- lowed by a solo and duet "When the shepherds," sung by Misses Higgins and N. Thompson, but where the con- nection with the operetta came in it was hard to tell, Miss Olive Roberts sang the solo, "Come from thy dwelling," with excellent taste, being an invocation to joy. The next was a descriptive quart Itte " 'Tis merry Christmas." by Misses 0. Clare (Joy), L. Barr (Peace), E. Bunting (Love), L. Longworth (Elope), followed by the chorus "Hail, all hail." la this the choir was heard to excellent advantage, the beautiful blending of the voices and their remarkably accurate balance being exceptionally well brought out. The altos were very fine. The solo "With my sisters three," Miss Olive Clare (Joy) preceded the duet, "Gentle Hope, your pretty secret whisper," by Misses L. Barr (Peace) and. Edith Bunting (Love). The solo "I have a secret," by Miss L.Leagworth (Elope) was very well sung,the action being also quite correct. The children, described as Kate (Miss Kate Asher)Bertie (Master H. Evans), Mirth (Miss M. Hipwood) are anxionsly awaiting the arrival of Santa Claus, but are greatly disappointed by the entry of th.e Frost King (Master Theo Clare) and plainly tell him that be is not wanted. Bertie would tolerate his presence if he weuld give him plenty of skating on Saturday afternoons, and the choir break out into the chorus "You surly old elf," which causes the frost king to throw aside his grimness and break out into laughter, and he departs to the chorus " To the mountains snowy crest." Al an interlude Miss Sarah Jones advances to the front and sings in an excellent manner " Watching for-Santa Slams." Scene 2, discloses a bedroom in which three children are asleep in bod and the goddess of dreams,Miss Corlett ndvancesand waving her wand over the bed, sings a lullaby, in splendid style, the children, Misses A. Hemmons, J. Picket and H. Houghton, beiag supposed to be in the land of dreams. Upon the depar- ture of the Goddess, three fairies, Misses A. Watkins, M. Jackson and M. Davies, enter and accompanied by. song perform some mystic passes over the children. The interval after their departure had the entry of Santa Claus is filled up by a pianoforte solo," Reindeer Gslop," which is illustrated by the sound of trotting .and the cracking of whips. Santa Claus (Mr. Burgess) accom- panied by his dwarfs Drako (Master W. Smith) and Krako (Master G. Sutton) enters the bedroom, and after filling the children's stockings and leaving other -presents take their departure. The children are suddenly , awakened and jumping out of bad discover the presents left them and immediately begin to make night hideous. In rush their parents who bid the children put away their toys and go to sleep. Scene 3, shows all the charac- ters again assembled expecting a visit from Santa Claus with Christmas presents.. His entry is heralded by the chorus" 0 Santa Claus," and he proceeds to distribute toys ad lib. This brought on the whistling chorus, and afterwards the concluding chorus" Our kind and loving father" which brought to a close, a pleasant and re- fined entertainment. The scenic effects were capitally carried out, the lime light being in charge of Mr. J. H. Graham. Miss M. Sudworth presided at the piano, Mr. Proudlove at the organ, and Mr. Bradley conducted the ' choruses, whilst Mr. Sandiford officiated as stage manager, prompter itc.

div.head: SABBATH KEEPING AND SABBA..CH B REAKING.
div.p: SABBATH KEEPING AND SABBA..CH B REAKING.
SERMON BY THE REV. W. H. DRUMMOND.

"Sabbath keeping and Sabbath breaking: A plea for a reasonable Sunday," was the subject of a discourse by , the Rev. W. H. Drummond in Cairo-street Chapel, on Sunday evening. He said so soon as any religious form had ceased to express real religion it should be dropped. He thought it might be statel ot the English Sunday that no religious institution was so universally ackeow- lodged among English people; that in relation te no other institution were they so powerfully restrained by the dead hand of the past ; that when freed from the bondage of formalism, no other institution was capable of such large usefulness in promoting the true interests of religion. Sunday, as they knew it, and still more as their grandfathers knew it was not the invention of English Puritanism, but it I was certainly one of its special prescriptions for human 1 1 salvation. Sunday at the present day was surrounded by a multitude of unwritten laws. There were many things which they shrank from doing, not because there was any harm in thern, but because they were supposed to be at variance with the peculiarly sacred character of the day. Sunday was still called by many the Sabbath, not in its beautiful old meaning, simply as the Rest Day, but as the day on which it was sinful to do things which were quite harmless on the other six days of the week. It was called the Lord's Day, as though every day from Monday to Saturday was not just as much a Lord's Day for holy living and divine service. 'I here was thus a great deal of confusion in the popular mind upon the meaning and obligation of Sun- day observance, and while probably a majority still ac- cepted current theories and practices, without thought or question, there was a growing minority who were perplexed and dissatisfied and leaked for a restaternant,a revision of belief and practice in regard to the whole question. They could no longer accept it as a form in- stituted by special divine command. They were no longer content simply to copy the religious habits of their forefathers. It it was still to commend their rever- ence it must be brought into s•eme intelligible rela- tion with existing needs and aspirations. As a form Sunday observance was good, helpful, and inepiring,but it was not to be confused with what was essential. Forms tended to separate themselves from their source, and to make claims of their owe upon human obedience. Sunday observance had done this in more ways than one,and te,that extent it had failed to help the growing life of aniseed. It appeared to him in no way helpful to re;igion, but quite the reverse, that museums and picture galleries and public reading roon's should be closed on Sunder:oer to encourage the belief that there was a peculiar sacredness attaching to Sunday which did not belong to every other day as well, to re- gard Sunday as a day of rest in a way that at all sug- gested that any work done was done in defiance of the Jaw of God, or to treat Sunday as a day on which the natural gaiety of home might fled no vent and the chil- dren were expected to eelace themselvee•for banished playthings with sentimental religieue story-books or badly drawn pictures of the patriarchs. But, on the otter hand,it appeared to him in every way heipful to re- ligion that there should curse one day in the week when the strain of care was relaxed, and the mind and hPa_rt could right themselves and be refreshed, and learn the ever new lesson that man did not live by bread alone, but by love and truth and goeduess and beeuty, the liv- ing words of God.

THE SEQUESTRATION ACTION. In the Court of Appeal on Tuesday, before the Lord Chief Justice and Lords Justices Lindley and A. L. Smith, the case of Fairclough v. the Manchester Ship Canal Company came on for hearing on appeal by the defendant Company from a decision of Mr. Justice Kekewich, who directed a writ of sequestration to issue for breach of an injunction restraining the Company from taking, for the purposes of the Ship Canal, a greater . .

quantity of ivater from the river Mersey than they were entitled to by Act of Parliament, M:. Moulton, Q.C., Mr. C. A. Cripps, Q.C., and Mr. 0. L. Clare appeared in suppnt of the appeal, and kr. Warmington, q.c., and Mr. A. T. Hughes for the respondenis. Mr. Moulton, in opening, said the short history of the matter was this. The Manchester Ship Canal Act per-

mitted the Company to do something subject to certain restrictions. The action was brougitt against his clients for having violated those restrictions, and by consent an injunction in the terms of the application was granted. Then a writ of sequestration was directed to issue for disobedience to that injunction and against this last order the present appeal was lodged. The Lord Chief Justice: The injunction prevented you taking more water than you were by is.w entitled

to. Mr. Moulton said that was so. The river Irwell fell into the canal before the Mersey did. Both then be- came merged into the canal, and continued so for a con- siderable distance. Then a point was reached at which the Mersey left the canal, and by a devious path got to Woolston Weir. It tumbled over tha ~and flowed along
the old rod of the river until it catna to.a place called
-11-o-w-fe-y Quay and to the Weir below, which' was called Howley Weir. Then it flowed on, and ultimately fell

Into the estuary. The Lord Chief Justice: Then at no part which is here in question is the canal coincident with the river? Mr. Moulton said it was not, except for a very short distance. Tha Lord Chief Justice: What is the situation of the plaintiff's mill ? Mr. Moulton said it was at Howley Weir. The mill- race was above, and the mill-tail was below. The Lord Chief Justice asked if thestatute was a limi- tation of the quantity of water be Ship Canal Com- pany were to take,or a reference to the quantity Messrs. Fairclough were to get. Mr.Moulton replied that it was a mixture of the two. It was primarily a limitation of the quantity the Com- pany took, but that depended upon the quantity of water that was going down. His clients were always al- lowed to take ten millions but supposing more than 100 million eubic feet of water was going down, they were allowed to take 15,000,000. However,for the purposes of this case their lordships might take it they were not en- titled to take more than 10,000,000 cubic feet in a day. Clause 88 of the original Ship Canal Act of 1885 stated that it was wanted for the protection of the Corporation of Warrington and the traders,manufacturers,and others carrying on business at or near Warrington. That would certainly include Messrs. Fairclough. Sub-section 12 was the limiting section. It gave the Ship Canal Company permission to take water from the Mersey above Warrington. but that permission was of a limited character. This limitation was first for the protection of Warrington, and secondly for the protection of such people as the plaintiffs. Damage of course must be done to the plaintiffs' mill in conseeaence of so much water being diverted. TheiLord Chief Justice: That does not follow, if you leave them sufficient. Ur. Moulton said perhaps he put it too strongly. He should not contend that diverting the water did not in- jure toe plaintiffs, but for that there was a specific compensation clause In the Act, which gave Messrs.Fair- dough compensation for all injury done to them by the works authorised by the Act. The Lord Chief Justice: That was on the Lands Clauses Act. It could not apply to your taking more water than you ought to. Mr. Moulton agreed that it did not cover any breach of their obligations. The Lord Chief Justice: /lave Messrs. Fairalough been compensated in fact? Mr. Moulton said they had received about £7,500, which he agreed covered more damage thaa they were entitled to compensation for under the Act. The Lord Chief Justice: The *hole question before us, however, is whether you took en one day more water than you had the right to take. Mr. Moulton': Yes, whether they had done something mere than the Act allowed. Under the Act the Ship Canal Company were entitled in any case to take 10,000,000 cable feet. They were entitled to take more than that under certain conditions of flow, but it might be taken that this was summer flow, and that they had no right to take more than 10,000,003. liThe Lord Chief Justice: Bo eou suggest that if the flew was much less than 100,000.000 cubic feet you would still be able to take 10,000,000? Mr. Moulton replied in the affirmative. It was the daily duty of the Ship Canal Company to so regulate the flow of water at the entrance to the canal that a greater q 'entity than the 10,000,000 was not taken during the twenty-four hours. Toe injunction granted against them in the first instance wee not resisted because at that time the path of the river was ,greatly impeded. There was the Butcher's Field Weir, which was now removed, and the Woolston Weir, which was in a very bad state indeed. The consequence was that the water had not a very bread alternative flaw down the river, and showed a tendency to ga down the canal. Woolsten Weir was reconstructed after the injunction was granted,and was composed of what were ktiewn as tilt:ng sluices. Ordin- ary sluices lifted up and down, the full pressure of the water being againie, them in their grooves. Tilting sluices turned on an axis, being, in fact, like a balanced valve. Prior to June 2 the weather had been exceed- inely dry, and the man in charge of Woolston Weir, thinking that enough water was not going over the Weir, opened the sluices. It was a blunder on his part, because these sluices should only be opened in flood weather, but he did net say this in the light of an ex- cuse. On the following day the man began to find the level of the water going down, and, being afraid the level of the canal would be lowered, for which he would certainly have caught it, he shut the whole of the sluices. The consequence wes that for a time unquestionably the weir was incapable of acting as a weir, and no water could got over until the level had been raised. Lord Justice Smith : Are you going to say that, calcu- lating these circumstances, the amount of water you took was less than 10,000,000? Mr. Moulton said the amount was much less than that. They were in a position to say exactly how much water went into the canal. Records were kept of the daily quantities. They kept a record of how many times the Latchford locks were used, and whether it was the whole lock or only a compartment of it. It was ad- mitted that no water flowed over or through the Latch- ford locks, and it was ee.sy to calculate exactly the lock- age water. Calculations made on the day the plaintiffs relied upon showed that the amount of water diverted into the canal was only about half the allowance to which they were entitled. Those ca:eulations were not disputed by the other side, but it was urged that the vast body of water unaccounted for got into the canal by leakage under the locks. The Lord Chief Justice: There must be a big leakage to account for five millions. Mr. Moulton: Mr. Justice Kekewich made the leakage amount to no less that 44 millions. On his findings of fact he found that 44 million cubic feet passed on the 2nd June. The total dry weather flow of the Thames before the intake of the water companies was only about fifty millions. The affidavit of Mr. Hunter, engineer in chief to the Ship Canal, stated the calculations arrived at from the records kept from day to day, and those cal- culations showed that on June 2 not nearly the ten millions passed into the canal. It was in reply to that that for the first time leakage was suggested by the other side. Lord Justice Lindley: When the injunction was granted was this theory as to leakage started? Mr. Moulton said it was not. The circumstances then were entirely different. The water was then allowed to flow eveieand through the sluices of Latchford As a matter of fact, when the injunction was granted there was a great deal to he done. Lord Justice Lindley: Then you have altered these weirs and so on since? Mr. Moulton: Yes. The case made on the other aide was that prier to the making of the Ship Canal there was always plenty of water for the purposes of the mill, but that afterwards there was not enough to keep the mill fully working, and that on the 2nd and 3rd of June they had to stop for some hours together. Lord Justice Smith: Flow did they make out that you were getting more than your ten millions P Mr. Moulton: !'hat we were letting more weer run over the sluices than we ought. Then there was an affi- davit by Mr. Longdin, who said he had known the river for a long time, and that he had teen accustomed to gauge it at Warrington Bridge, which was belosvcElow- ley Weir. He gave as the minimum dry-weather flow 70 million cubic feet, and he sought to jestify that by saying that the gatieing in August of 1888 was 74 mil- lions. In cross-examination he got from Mr. Longdin that June and July of that year were exceptionally wet, so that it would hardly be fair to accept the minimum dry-weather flow An such data. The minimum dry- weather flow meant the emallest tow that bad ever been known. The only points relied upon by the learned judge in.arriving at his judgment was the minimum dry-weather flow of 70 millions, which Me; Longdin spoke to, and Mr. Faircloteeh's statement that he had often been short ef water. fie would call their Lord- ship's attention to the fact that in July of the year in which Mr. Longdin made his dry-weather calculation as to flow there was a rainfall of nearly six inches, while the May rainfall of 1898 was only a third of an inch. Flo pressed that fact on the leerned judge in the court be- low, because it proved they could not take as the mini- mum dry flow a year in which the rainfall was so great, and that it more than threw doubt upon the 70 million cubic feet per day as the minimum dry-weather
The Lord Chief Jugticm : A.ssuruing that . you have given us an outline of -Vie position accurrately, I think we should like to hear what the other side have to say.

Mr. Moulton said Mr. Justice Kekewich, having gone into the question of minimum now, and this being a matter which was life or death to his clients, he had thought it right to file further evidence with regard to that questionsand he should ask leave to nse it. It was clearly: he7ond the power of the Ship Canal Compcny to provide 70 millions as the minimum dAily The Lord Chief Justice : It is clearly not your duty te provide 70 millions. Your duty is not to take more _ _

than 10 millions. Mr. Moulton said he felt bound to show their-Lord- ships something more satisfactory as to the dry-weather flow than he was enabled to do in tile court below. Lord Justice Smith: What do your witnesses say? Mr. Moulton : From 20 to 22 millions as the
lutely dry-weather flow. The witnesses are of the highest reputation and experience with regard to these

matters. Leave having been given to use this fresh evidence, Mr. Moulton proceeded to read tke evidence of Sir Ben- jamin Baker, who stated that 70 million cubic feet of water per day as the minimum dry-weather flow was a physical impossibility. He knew of no river in this country where such a quantity was even approached as a dry-weather minimum. The estimate of Mr. Lengdin was apparently based,not on a series of measures,bat on one mew ure taken in August, 1888. Having regard to the rainfall of the previous two months, it was quits possible the discharge was about that amount, but it was quite impossible that this should represent the mini- mum flow.

Another witness was Mr. Mansergh, an engineer who had specially devoted himself to waterworks, and was chosen one of the three engineers appointed on the Royal Commission to inquire into the London water supply. He stated that the dry-weather flow of the Mersey could not be more than that of the Thames' and was probably less. Taking it, however, at the Thames figure, the dry-weather minimum would be 11.-i million cubic feet

per day. Another witness'wlso was unable to agree with Mr. Longdin's figures was Mr. George Henry Hill, who had superintended the bringing of Thirlmere water into Manchester, and who. was also engaged in bringing Loch

Katrine water into Glasgow. On the other side there was the evidence of Mr. J. Wolfe Barry, who said that any comparison between the Thames an the Mersey Wad fallacious and illusory. The average rainfall in the basin of the Thames was 27 inches whereas in the basin of the Mersey it was 39. Of the former only one-third was carried away by drainage,the remainder being disposed of by evaporation, while in the case of the Mersey only one-half of the rainfall was evaporated. The Lord Chief Justice said Mr. Barry did not deal with the minimum dry-weather flow, but simply made a comparison between the Thames and the Mersey. Mr. Moulton said that was sc—Counsel proceeded to read further affidavits of Mr. Longdin, surveyor, of Warrington, and Mr. Burgess, formerly an aiderman of the same town, in reply to the evidence filed on behalf of the Ship Canal Company, concluding by remarking that there was no answer to that which the defendants had swum to, and that the defendants had not shown there had been any breach of the injunction. Mr. Hughes, in reply to the Lerd Chief Justice, said he admitted that in the first instance the onus was open his clients of proving that the Canal Company had taken more water than the statute allowed. He should, how- ever, submit that the onus was upen the other side at the point when their Lordships,upon the evidence, came to the conclusion that there had been a reduction of the dry-weather fl .w the river from 70 millions. Lord Justice Lindley : Is that the right way to do it P _ _ . . .

The problem to be solved is what they have taken. Mr. Hughes : Of course that might be arrived at in one of two ways—either by measure, if that was a pos- sible mode,which they did not admit,o- by inference of the facts. According to our case it i. not a matter of practical meßsurenient. The Lord Chief Justice: Apart from leakage, why not?
Mr. Hughes: Apart from leakage, perhaps. The Court then adjourned until Wednesday. SECOND DA!. YROCEE DINGS.

In the Court of Appeal on Wednesday before the Lord Chief Justice and Lerd Justices Lindley and A. L. Srnith,the hearing was resumed of the case of Fairclough v. the Manchester Ship Canal Company. The ground of the appeal was that, so far from disobeying the in- juaction, the Company had, on June 2, the date named in the plaintiffs' statement of claim, taken for the pur- vets of their undertaking only about half of the ten million cubic feet of water to which by statute they were entitled. _ _

• Mr. Fletcher Moulton, Q.C., Mr. riripps, Q.C., and Mr. Clare appeared in support of the appeal, and Mr. War mington Q.C., and Mr. Hughes for tbe respondents. Mr. Warmington, Q.C., in opening the case for the respondents, said their case was this. They had been the proprietors of a mill upon the river Mersey for a period of tweety-one years, which mill was worked by water-power derived from the Mersey, there being two water-wheels for that purpose. Until the canal was constructed, there never was a stoppage of the mill from want of water. The minimum amount of water required to work the mill was 45 million cubic feet per twenty-four hours. Ho would point out that the defend- ants had not produced a single person who had a prac- ti eat working upon the river Mersey; no millowner, no person who had used the river prior to the con- struction of the canal was called on behalf of the defend- ants. Lord Juatiee Smith: But the defendants don't guaran- tee any (lea yof water ? Mr. Warnenigton : I submie they do. I say that on the construction of the Act of Parliament they guarantee that the flow of the river shall continue as before, !Rubject only to the deduction mentioned in the clause. That means to say that the flow shall not be dimin- ished by a larger volume than was mentioned in section 88. The Lord Chief Justice : That is agreed. Mr. Warmington : Therefore to that extant they do guarantee. The Lord Chief Justice: Where? Mr. Warrnington : If the flow does not exceed one bundle d millions they are not entitled to take more than ten millions. Lord Justice 'insith : But suppose you have two ab- normally dry years and no water comes down the river at all? Mr. Wartniagton : There never was such a case. Lord Justice Smith: But I am only taking your proposition that they guarantee a certain quantity of water. Lord Justice Lindley: Do they guarantee anything? Mr. Warmingten : Yes, sty Lord. The Lord Cnief Justice : That seems te go to the root of the matter. Mr.Warmington said he should like to call attention to the terms of section 88, "The Company shall not within any twenty-four houre abstract or divert from the river Mersey " Lord Justice Smith : Don't you read "into the cane' ?" Mr. Warmington : I do not care whether it is into the canal or anywhere else. Below a certain point called A the Mersey is the canal, and the canal is the Mersey. Now see what the other words are "Nor allow the flow therefrom." That sfiows that they have the control of the river Mersey below point A. The Lord Chief Justice : Is that anything different from that they "shall net divert from the river Mersey ?" Mr. Warmington : Yes, because we have the wort " flow." Mv submission is, that means they are to keep the flow ofithe river Mersey. They are not allow to flow therefrom into the canal such a quantity of water as to diminish the downward flow of the river past Howley Quay'. The Lord Chief Justice : " By greater quantity ?" Mr. Warmington : Yes ; they are not to take more than 10 million cubic feet from the flow of the river past Howley Quay in any 24 hours. The Lord Chief Justice: What the Company say is that the reading of this is that where the quantity of water in cubic feet flows down the river past Howley Quay in any 24 hours does not exceed 100 millions,they shall not be entitled to take more than 10 millions. Mr. Warmineton :It means that, I agree but I think it means something more. I want to make this extra point; first, as to whether they are entitled to impound at all—that is to say, impound the river. It is a most important point. Your lordships have heard what the result is. On the 2nd Juno they stopped our mill for pretty well the whole day. They impounded from nine in the morning until three the next morning. They stopped the flow altogether. Is that consistent with the section, which says chey are not to "allow to flow there- , from " ? I should have thought that implied that the flow was to continue. The lewd Chief Justice : I think you must also read in connection with that a' by a greater quantity than." Mr. Warmingten : Yes," by a greater quantity than ten millions if the flow past Howley Quay is 100 milliona," but what my learned friend is doing is stopping the flow 01 the river past Howley Quay alto- gether. Lord Justice Smith : Suppose there were ten million cubic feet fiewing down the Mersey, do you say they must not take their ten millions? Mr. Warmington : They could use it perhaps,but they would not be entitled to impound it in using it. It was never intended they should. The Lord Chief Justice : But you had the benefit two days before the water was impounded. Mr. Warmingtnn replied that it was no benefit to his clients. They wanted 45 million cubic feet day by day, and it was nonsense to give them 15 millions one day and

5 the next. The 75 could not be used. Any quantity i'nve f he
Mr. Warmington : No. The Lord Chief Justice If the Company's conten- tion is right, you will probably have to construct reser- voirs.

Mr. Warmington • If their contention is right,it means that if the flow of the river is brought down to ten mil- Bons they take all, and we get none, ani yet their ten was to be measured by something that never passed Howley Quay. Was that the true construction of the Act of Parliament? Lord Justice Smith: What happened then will prob- ably never happen again. Mr. Warmington: Our mills have been stopped day' after day simply by what the defendants have done. Lord Justice Lindley : How do you propose to make out that they are abstracting from the river Mersey ond diverting into the canal more than the ten -nillions to which they are by Act entitled? , Mr. Warmington: I ray my case comes within the words " nor allow to flow therefrom into the canal.' When they impound they impound in the canal, and for the purpose of this section, where the river and the canal are one, they impound in the canal because they stop the flow. Lord Justice.Lindley : Suppose they construct a dam at point A. It would stop your mill; but would you have any remedy? Mr. Warmington : Yes, I submit, because they would stop the flow of the river past Howley Quay. The Lord Chief Justice said the plaintiffs had been paid a sum which would compensate them for the stop- page of the mill far one day. Mr. Warmington said it was a matter not of one day in a year, but of four or five times in a fortnight. Mr. Moulton: We have never pounded up since that one occasion.
Mr. Warmink ton said it was being done still.
Mr. Moulton-: Excuse me; I think not not

The Lord Chief Justice: What do you say follows this construction of yours? Do you say that if the flow is merely enough to satisfy your 45 millions per day that they are bound to divert all the rest? Mr. Warmington : No; I have limited my point to this, that what they are entitled to do is to abstract flowing water, and not to stop the water flowing. After some further:arguenent,Mr.Warmington proceeded to deal at length with the evidence given on affidavit, He said that the plaintiff's case was supported by essen- tially practical men, who had a large expereuce of the river Mersey. There was the plaintiff, Mr. Fairclough, Mr. Robinson, who lived at Warrington, Mr. Burgess, who resided in the same town, and Mr. Longdin, who, he supposed, would be regarded as an expert witness. Confirmatory evidence had also been given by Mr. Miller, who from 1863 to ' 1868 was manaeer at the Mersey Mills. Dealing with the affidavits on the other side, he desired to call attentien to the fact that Mr. Hill gauged the flow of the river on the 27th of May , which happened to be a Sunday. Now Mr. Hill knew, anti everybody knew, that in all the calculations made on behalf of the plaintiff Sunday calculations were ex- cluded, in order to be fair. It was on Sunday that reser- vairs or lodges were filled, and it would be ntost mislead- ing to take Sunday as a fair sample of the flow of the river. He suggested that the evidence taken as a whole , justified his assertion that the minimum flow before the

conetructien of the canal was something in excess of 74,000,000 cubic feet. The Lord Giles Justice: New the point ie, what was the flaw after? Nith the flew belnw 100,000,000, did the defendants take more than 10,000,000? Mr. Warmington : We have got this. In 1833, at the end of May, after a rainfall in March, April, and May of 3.91, there were 54 million cubic feet of water pass- ing down. Now eompare that with the state of things vihich,according to the defendants' own statements.now exists. In March, April and May. with a rainfall of 7ZI, the flow is 21-22 million cubic feet;• so that with a rainfall nearly double, the flow is less than half. The Lord ChiefJustieo: How is the difference made ? Is it accounted for by greater abstraction, or how ? Mr. Warmington : That the defendants have not shown. I submit it is enough for us to have shown this immense diminution to call for an answer. The Lord Chief Justice: Of course you are not in a Ipasition to check the actual consumption, and they are. Mr. Warmington called attention to their replies. In the first place, they aid not deign to notice the earlier flow of the river at all. They contented themselves with saying that on these days in June the locks at Lel:Alford were used so many times, and they totalled op the amount of water used in the lockage, and said that was all they had used. His lea.reed friend had added to that the amount impounded by raising the level of Latchford locks to point Aon the 2nd June. His case was that, taking that particular day, the raising of the water level was 8 inches. That was clear from their own records. Calculating on the defendants' own bails of a rise of 5 inches, the quantity of water impounded was 31 million cubic feet. On the assumption that the rise was 8 inches and not five, the amount would come to six millions. Then to that had to be added the amount the defendants a.dmttted they took through the feeder. the Latchford Canal, which was 4 millions. Now, nothing was added for the space between VVoolston Weir and point A, which was made part of the impound. They prevented it flawing down the river, and this amounted to another 11, millions, making up a deprivationof about eleven millions. He was raying this to show how he could prove the actual deprivation by the plaintiffs on the 2nd June.

_ Lord Justice Smith: Then what became of the enor- mous balance of water not accounted for? Mr. Warmington : That, of course, I cannot say. Lord Justice Smith : Before this case is conclud shall want to know. Mr. Warmington had not concluded his argumentd when the Court rose for the day.

div.head: THURSDAY'S IPROCEEDINGS.
div.p: THURSDAY'S IPROCEEDINGS.

The Lord Chief Justice and Lords Justices Lindley and A. L. Smith on Thursday, in the Court of Appeal, re- sumed the hearing of the case of Fairclough and Sons v. the Manchester Ship Canal Company. In the absence of Mr. Warmington, Mr. Hughes re- sumed the arguments on behalf of the plaintiffs. The Lord Chief Justice said that if the learned counsel had any thing te add upon the construction of the statute they would be glad to hear it first. Mr. Efughes said that was what he proposed to do. It would be seen that section 35, which was the enabling clause, provided that the Company " may, subject as hereinafter mentioned, divert into and impound in the canal," and so on, the waters of the Irwell, the Mersey, and other rivers. That, of course, must be read in the first in,ta.nce, no doubt, with regard to the preamble, and that preamble stated, " Whereas it is expedient that the Compa.ny be enabled, subject to the provisions of this Act, and for the purposes of the canal and works by thi3 Act authorised, to enter upon, take, and use the bed, channel, and banks of the river Mersey, Irwell," and so forth, so that the enabling was only to the extent necessary for the works intended by ' the Act. Further, section 32 was limited in this way, " subject as hereinafter mentioned," and that was a reference, no doubt, amens, other clauses to section 88, sub-section 12. Section 88' provided that "the Com- pany seen not, within any 24 hours, abstract or divert from the river Mersey, nor allow to flow therefrom into the canal, such a quantity of water as will diminish the flow of the river past Howley Quay by greater quanti- ties than ten million cubic feet in any 24 hours," His submission upon that was that the Company was only enabled to take subject to that limitation, and that they were not to reduce the flow of the river past Howley Quay by more than ten million cubic feet. Now, the river so far as Warrington was concerned was the river at or below Howley Quay, and the mods in which the water was taken, whether by diversion or abstraction, was quite immaterial to Warrington. Their only con- cern was to have the flew of the river at or below How- ley Quay,and he should contend that if in any day there would have been a certain quantity flowing past Howley Quay, which, by reasons of the operations of the Com- pany, had been reduced by more than ten million cubic feet, then there was a breach of the provisions of the section. The Lord Chief Justice : Suppose only ten millions was going down, would the Company be entitled to use that ten millions ? Mr. Hughee : Probably they would. The Lord Chief Justice : Supposing the quantity was fifteen millions, would they be entitled to use ten and send down the other five ? Mr. Hughes; I think so, my Lord. Lord Justice Smith: Suppose they could not obtain ten millions without damming up the river at 'Woolston ; do you say they could do that? Mr. Hughes ; I do not think I aye concerned to answer that question, because such a thing has never hap- pened. I should therefore prefer not to deal with that question. The Lord Chief JUatice : We came back to the ques- tion—Did they take more than the ten millions to which they were entitled ? Mr. Hughes ea.id,on the figures,he submitted they had. There was a vast difference between the present and past conditions of the flow of the 'river at Howley quay. It was not for the plaintiffs to account for that differ- ence. If it was for the plaintiffs to snake a suggestion, they did suggest, and what they suggested was that the reach of the canal from Irlam to Latchford was not water-tight. The evidence they had upon that showed that the canal for a distance of 500 yards above Latch- ford, and for a long distance below, was cut through sandstone rock of a very porous and friable character, and .which was full of cracks and fissures. The evidence on the other side as regarded that point included an affidavit by Mr. Hunter, in which he said that the rock though soft was dense and bomogenous, and almost en- tirely free from cracks and fissures. That, he ventured to think, was entirely disproved, and they had in their possessioa early photographs, which showed steam nav- vies ploughing through the rock. Mr. Moulton : Steam navvies taking up the debris after blasting. Mr: Hughes referred to the evidence of Mr. Brown, resident engineer to the Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway, and formerly reaident engineer for the construction of Latchford locks, who stated that the subsnil consisted of soft, friable, and very porous red sandstone, which was full of cracks and fissures, and of such a nature as to permit considerable leakage. ge
1 (Mr. Brown) recommended the Canal Company to con- struct a long concrete apron, and brick the sides of the

_ canal. The learned counsel concluded by saving that tha matter was one of very great importance to his clients, and he wished to reiterate that it was not a question of a few days, though they were bound in bringing the action to choose particular lays. The complaint viss general. The Lord Chief Justice: Your case is that the de• fondants have systematically taken more than tem

Mr. Hughes: Yes, my Lord. M. Moulton on rising to reply was asked by the Llrd Chief Justice if there was any explanatioa of the cir- cumstances which led to consent being given to the ii junction. Mr. Moulton said there was not.

The Court having adjourned for lunch, and on their lordships'return the Lord Chief Justice said the Court did feel that the weight of evidaace pointed to a consider- able diminution in the dry-weather flow since the com- pletion of the canal works than was previously the case. If Mr. Moulton had any observation to make on that matter the Court would be glad to hear it.

Mr. Moulton said it was not by any MRAUS necessary for him to say, nor did the materials before him justify him in sayino, that .there had, been no change in the distribution of the flow. He thought Mr. Longdin pat it rightly in thinking that the flools of the different rivers now travelled at a greater rate, and where It times there was a larger flow than formerly there was also at times a much smaller flow than formerly. The Lord Chief Justice: That is all you can say ? Mr. Moulton : Yes.
The Lord Chief Justice : Then Ido not think we re• quire to hear anything further. We will take time to consider our decision.

THE PARISH COUNCIL MEETING.—A meeting of Council was held on Friday night, undef the presidency of Mr. A. Guest. There were also present—Messrs. James Ford, D. Summerville, J. Tudor, T. Grounds, and James Collier (clerk), Mr. C. L. Evans, of Norton, acknowledged receipt of a complaint from the Council, with reference to the dangerous state of the pit on the road leading from Weston to Clifton Mr. Evans prom- ised to look into the matter when ho came to Wes%os• There was no ether business of interest. SONS or TESIPERANCE.—&C the fortnightly meetin! 0 the above order, '.teld in the Sons of Temperance Hall. Weston, Mr. Thomas J. Holt, of Runcorn, read a paper on "Friendly Societies." Mr. George Holt, of Runcorn, was invited to preside. After a paper was read,a discus- sion took place, in which Bros Walker, Cotterill, Hazle. hurst, J. Brown, S. Dodd and D. Kirkham took part. A vote of thanks was passed to Bro. Holt for his paper, to which he replied, and a pleasant evening we then brought to a close.

A PfIASE OF TILE _EDUCATION QUESTION.

Sir,—At present there is a lull in the storm of politi- cal warfare, but like everything else connected with this world it is not oh a permanent character, and before Parliament meets the storm will be raging as fiercely aS ever it did.

_ The battle will centre round the oducetion question. We have been told that this is a qeestion which is Rot difficult to settle,only that there are so many people who bother about it, who have no right to. Sir John Gore is one of suck persons. He said, in effect, that the con- troversy does not exist in the mho'', but outside. We, that may be, but as the money comes from the pockets of the ratepayers and as they are Englishmen, and as Englishmen are business people, they very naturally ask if you spend our money, surely we have a right to ask, what is it going to he used for, and whether it is going to be spent properly? Of course the managers and teachers of the school will not abject to receive 'iextrei payment. To the teachers it will probably mean an lc* crease of salary. The difficulty however, does not lie in that direction; it is not merely an increase in the amount of money that is the trouble. We cannot afford to be in any respects niggardly regarding education, bemuse upon it depends very largely the supremacy Of commercial life, to say nothing of the advantages it confers in other directions. The difficulty of this question is—religion. It is veil hard to have to record 'against religion that it hinder,' education, but to judge by the past it does de so. That ,is the part which is so irritating. If ever there is argument between two persons, they almost come, to [blows over the religious point of the jealous lest Nonconformist children should imbibe super- stion, another lest denominational c hildren shoul6i grew up into til nted with

of the denomination. The position is truly difficult. Partizanship is rife. Impartial judgment is difficult to form, and to all aP' pearances there is every prospect of a battle of religious than which no one can conceive of anything more bittLr and more un•Chrialike. I have yet to be convinced that it is religion that is the" irritant." Tbe burden of Christianity is peace and goodwill. Either the angelic message of long ago is a lie,or else Christianity is somewhat different to wh‘t was then. Which of the two is it? Perhaps the latter suggestion is the correct one. The religion ef to-day nothing better than a set of creeds, sects, etc., the per tizans of which can see nothing beyond the small circle of their own manufactured Christianity. They forge that the great question is not merely to believe, but to live up to its principles. The solution of this question can only be the exclusion of dogmatic teaching from schools. We shall have to treat religion as a luxury ; if you waist it you must pal, for it. This is a drastic proposal, but it is the oni.7, strictly fair solution. It is not a solution which Wit give satisfaction,but the contending clamour is so gritatt that it is the only one that will for ever end the queS*. tion.—Yours truly,
